paragraphs.text: Although flow-accelerated corrosion (FAC) has been studied for more than five decades worldwide and its main scientific influences are well known, translating that knowledge into practice at fossil, combined-cycle/HRSG and nuclear plants has fallen short: serious failures continue, at essentially the same locations seen in the 1980s and 1990s. The review covers current mechanistic theory, the main plant locations of FAC, the surface features that identify single-phase and two-phase FAC, the cycle chemistries in use and the principal monitoring tools for detecting FAC. It also describes management, inspection, prediction and chemistry measures for stopping FAC and explains how the required approach differs between fossil, HRSG and nuclear plants.

The economic burden of metallic corrosion is very large. A two-year study that also counted prevention costs estimated the 2002 total across all US industries at 276 x 10^9 USD [1]. For the US power sector alone, a 2001 report put the 1998 cost at 17 x 10^9 USD, roughly 7.9 % of what consumers paid for electricity, with about 22 % judged avoidable through practical, cost-effective measures [2]. Among corrosion types in power plants, FAC of carbon steel has been labelled a "major issue" for nuclear units [3] and a "major problem" across nuclear, fossil and industrial plants [4]. For 1987, the FAC monitoring and prevention costs of a US nuclear plant were estimated at an average of 100 000 USD per outage [5], and as late as 2014 FAC was identified as the leading cause of damage and failure in HRSGs of combined-cycle plants [6].

Corrosion research on boiler systems dates back to the early 1900s. FAC, then generally called erosion-corrosion (E-C), was blamed in the 1940s for a number of failures of carbon steel power plant and industrial piping; these cases were poorly documented and treated as maintenance matters, with pipes replaced and operation restarted. Several studies on FAC appeared by the 1960s [7-9], and by the 1980s the phenomenon was thought to be adequately understood, partly because parallel research during the 1970s in Germany, France, Russia and the United Kingdom on nuclear and steam turbine issues seemed to have dealt with the main concerns. No serious damage was reported in the 1970s, and neither the first major single-phase FAC case at the Navajo fossil plant in Arizona in 1982 [10] nor a comparable event at the Trojan pressurized water reactor (PWR) in 1985 [11] prompted serious attention.

That confidence ended in 1986 when four workers died at the Surry nuclear plant [12], after the 457 mm (18 inch) feedwater pump suction line failed at a 90 ° elbow, severely wall-thinned by FAC, suffered a guillotine break. A subsequent USNRC bulletin [13] listed 34 US nuclear plants (one HTGR, six BWRs and 27 PWRs) with FAC experience over 1967-1986, typically in six kinds of single-phase water systems and six kinds of two-phase steam-water systems. Surry triggered an international effort to understand FAC at the plant level: many research programmes followed, inspection and non-destructive evaluation (NDE) systems were developed, and this ultimately led to a number of computer codes and models supporting data management and inspection protocols.

Despite this greater research effort, FAC incidents in nuclear and fossil power did not decline, showing that how serious and complex FAC is in high energy systems had again been underrated. Since 1986 three further accidents caused by FAC in single-phase water have killed plant workers: Pleasant Prairie (1995) [14,15], Mihama (2004) [16] and Iatan (2007) [17], and many two-phase steam-water FAC incidents without injury have also occurred. Table 1 lists these major incidents, all in single-phase flow; the earlier Navajo fossil and Trojan nuclear failures are included for comparison even though nobody died, because large diameter pipes ruptured. The FAC mechanism and these and other plant occurrences are discussed in Section 4.

A new generating technology, the combined-cycle gas turbine (CCGT) with an HRSG, appeared in the mid-1900s, beginning with the first commercial unit at Belle Isle, Oklahoma, USA, in 1949, and such units are now installed worldwide in very large numbers. FAC rapidly became the main availability problem of HRSGs, with numerous single- and two-phase failures, and remains so today [19]. Water constraints have recently led many combined-cycle and fossil plants to adopt air-cooled condensers (ACC); these carbon-steel heat exchangers have very large surface areas, have suffered FAC, and generate large quantities of corrosion products that foul the circuits [20].

Interest in FAC appears to be reviving as operators worldwide seek lower costs, higher efficiency and better safety. Since 2007 additional research, plant assessments and laboratory work have been carried out, and new prediction codes and inspection techniques have been produced. The International Atomic Energy Agency coordinated an international benchmarking of leading calculation methods in 2012 [21], and there have been four international conferences on FAC in nuclear plants and two on fossil/combined-cycle plants, making a comprehensive review timely.

The review mainly aims to update the authors' earlier reviews, one on fossil and combined-cycle plants [18] and one critiquing accepted FAC mechanisms [22], and to condense recent work into a concise picture of FAC mechanisms and their implications for control in operating plants. The authors stress that FAC science is now much better understood (Section 2), is neither random nor mysterious, and can readily be applied to all steam/electric generating plants. The paper concentrates on FAC in conventional fossil feedwater circuits, in the feedwater, economizer and evaporator circuits of combined-cycle/HRSG units, and in air-cooled condensers, and the paper presents for the first time in one document the damage causes and remedies for vulnerable systems. Nuclear plants, where FAC is systematically documented by industry, regulatory and utility bodies, receive less detail. The same understanding has been applied in worldwide assessments of steam generating plants serving industries including oil refineries, chemical works, pulp and paper mills, dairies, LNG facilities and desalination plants.

These assessments show that cycle chemistry strongly controls and influences FAC. For fossil and combined-cycle plants, the newest IAPWS documents [23-26] give guidance on optimizing chemistry to greatly reduce or eliminate FAC, and many of their principles also apply to nuclear plants. Tools are now available that let operators identify the key chemistry shortcomings, termed repeat cycle chemistry situations (RCCS), which will cause FAC if not corrected (Section 7.6).

Section 2 summarizes the main factors behind FAC in power plants, including new mechanistic findings, as background for the plant observations in later sections; fuller reviews exist elsewhere [27,28]. FAC is generally understood to be governed by the oxide film on carbon steel, which acts as a diffusion barrier. Because dissolved iron species move from the surface into the flowing bulk water, the mass transport behaviour of the flow is important and is commonly assumed to be controlling (Section 2.5). With the oxide dissolving into the water while metal oxidation replaces it, the film reaches a steady-state thickness, and a thicker, more compact film gives a stronger diffusion barrier and better protection. The following subsections examine how oxide properties and flow affect FAC and argue that explanations relying only on mass transfer and fluid flow are incomplete, since the oxide's properties and dissolution kinetics must also be taken into account.

paragraphs.section: 2.1 General Corrosion of Carbon Steel and Oxide Formation
paragraphs.text: Corrosion of carbon steel in static or slow-moving high temperature water relevant to boilers was assessed in the 1930s [29], giving the classic curve of relative attack rate at 310 °C against pH25°C (adjusted with strong base or acid), which has a minimum near pH25°C 11 [30] and confirmed the rationale for high pH treatment of coolant systems. Autoclave tests showed that the steel forms a double-layered magnetite corrosion product film, the Potter-Mann double layer [32]: a fine-grained inner layer of 30–50 nm crystallites [31] adjacent to the metal that acts as a diffusion barrier, covered by an outer layer of 1–10 µm crystallites. The inner layer grows at the metal-oxide interface (M-O), filling the volume of corroded metal, while the outer layer precipitates at the oxide-solution interface (O-S), so the boundary between the two layers marks the original metal surface.

paragraphs.section: 2.1 General Corrosion of Carbon Steel and Oxide Formation
paragraphs.text: Castle and Masterson's pores-solution model [33] proposes that in high temperature water (~ 300 °C) under reducing, mildly alkaline conditions, pores in the oxide let the water oxidant reach the metal. At the confined M-O, roughly 50 % of the iron that corrodes ends up as the fine-grained inner magnetite (the oxide-to-metal volume ratio, or Pilling-Bedworth ratio, being 2.1), and the remainder diffuses out through the pores to the O-S, where it precipitates as the outer layer of solution-grown, often octahedral, magnetite crystals. The model reproduces the parabolic corrosion kinetics of steel fairly well. Robertson [34] objected, chiefly because the corrosion activation energy (120 kJ · mol^-1) far exceeds typical aqueous diffusion values (~ 15 kJ · mol^-1); he instead suggested that water reaches the M-O via micropores but that the rate-controlling step is outward solid-state diffusion of iron ions along oxide grain boundaries.

paragraphs.section: 2.1 General Corrosion of Carbon Steel and Oxide Formation
paragraphs.text: For the neutral to mildly alkaline (pH25°C up to about 11), reducing or low oxygen environments of aqueous power systems, the metal-oxide interface reactions are: Fe = Fe^2+ + 2e^- (1) (iron is oxidized to ferrous ions, releasing electrons); 2H_2O + 2e^- = 2H· + 2OH^- (2) (water is reduced to hydrogen atoms and hydroxide ions).

paragraphs.section: 2.1 General Corrosion of Carbon Steel and Oxide Formation
paragraphs.text: At high temperature in alkaline media such as reactor primary coolants, the hydrogen atoms from Eq. (2) diffuse into the metal; where the steel forms the fluid's containment, they recombine at its outer surface and escape to the atmosphere: 2H· = H_2 (3) (two hydrogen atoms combine to a hydrogen molecule). This gas evolution is quantitative, and measuring it has served to determine steel corrosion rates in high temperature lithiated water [31] and underpins a non-intrusive instrument for monitoring piping corrosion rates in aqueous systems [35]; at the lower temperatures and conditions of feedwater systems, however, hydrogen effusion into the metal probably differs.

paragraphs.section: 2.1 General Corrosion of Carbon Steel and Oxide Formation
paragraphs.text: How the anodic sites (Eq. (1)) and cathodic sites (Eq. (2)) and the resulting hydrogen generation are distributed on the corroding surface governs the morphology of the oxide that first forms [36]. When the hydrogen from Eq. (2) effuses through the metal, a tightly knit oxide results [37]; when the steel is fully immersed in the fluid, the hydrogen atoms collect in interstitial sites of the metal matrix until an equilibrium level is reached, after which hydrogen diffuses outward into the fluid and a more porous oxide grows. In strongly alkaline media (for example 15 % NaOH), the high corrosion rates yield very porous oxides and most hydrogen goes to the fluid [37].

paragraphs.section: 2.1 General Corrosion of Carbon Steel and Oxide Formation
paragraphs.text: At the M-O, magnetite is produced from one half of the Eq. (1) ferrous ions together with the hydroxide ions of Eq. (2): Fe^2+ + 2OH^- = Fe(OH)_2 (4) (ferrous ions and hydroxide form ferrous hydroxide), followed by the Schikorr reaction [38]: 3Fe(OH)_2 = Fe_3O_4 + 2H_2O + H_2 (5) (ferrous hydroxide converts to magnetite, water and hydrogen). Eq. (5) is oxidative at both the M-O and the O-S and produces hydrogen that diffuses to the bulk water.

Unlike these mechanisms, which apply in fairly static solutions saturated with dissolved iron, FAC takes place where the oxide tends to dissolve, because the solution is under-saturated in dissolved iron so that Eq. (5) does not proceed at the O-S, and where the flow is turbulent, which accelerates corrosion. Under-saturation usually arises as the fluid passes through a temperature gradient that raises iron solubility. The resulting magnetite is thin, with hardly any outer precipitate, and the thinner it is, the weaker the protection and the higher the FAC rate. Plant and laboratory observations confirm that high FAC rates go with thin oxides; Figure 1 demonstrates this inverse relation with oxide thickness data for 0.06Cr0.01Mo0.19Cu steel measured behind a nozzle or ferrule in laboratory feedwater tests [39].

A steady state is reached when magnetite formation at the M-O matches dissolution at the O-S, giving a constant FAC rate. Dissolution is the reverse of Eq. (5): Fe_3O_4 + 2H_2O + H_2 = 3Fe(OH)_2 (6) (magnetite is reductively dissolved by hydrogen to ferrous hydroxide), so it is a reductive process. The hydrogen generated by Eq. (5) at the M-O and diffusing through the oxide equals precisely what is required at steady state to dissolve magnetite reductively by Eq. (6) at the O-S. Figure 2 summarizes these processes within the oxide film during FAC; the scheme is widely accepted as the basic principle of FAC and corresponds to the pores-solution model for steel in iron-saturated water [33], except that the oxide dissolves at the O-S instead of precipitating.

Eqs. (1), (2), (4) and (5) describe electrochemical steps governed by the system's electrochemical corrosion potential, while Eq. (6) is tied to Eq. (4). Under steady-state conditions the film thickness is constant and mass balances give Eq. (1) = (2) + (3) and Eq. (2) = (4) + (6) (the rates of the coupled reactions balance one another). The Figure 3 cross-section SEM image of oxide on a test specimen corroded by FAC in ~ 300 °C reactor primary coolant agrees with the Figure 2 scheme.

FAC is strongly influenced by fluid chemistry, temperature and flow. Attack is fast at 130–150 °C, and the temperature effect grows as the flow rate increases (Figure 4). Magnetite solubility changes in step (Figure 5), reflecting that the mechanism depends on magnetite film dissolution. Since Figure 5 shows solubility at usual feedwater temperatures falling as ammonia-controlled pH rises, FAC rates drop with greater alkalinity, and practical feedwater systems therefore run at pH25°C of about ~ 8.8 to ~ 9.8, depending on whether copper alloys are present in the circuit.

Under nuclear reactor primary coolant conditions of ~ 300 °C, by contrast, FAC rates rise as pH25°C increases beyond ~ 10 with a strong base such as LiOH, which supports the oxide dissolution mechanism because magnetite solubility, though fairly low, increases in that range [43] (Figure 6). CANDU primary coolant system operators (typically 265 to 310 °C) are therefore now advised to set the Li concentration so that pH25°C sits at the low end of the specified alkalinity range (dissolved Li of 0.5 x 10^-4 to 2.0 x 10^-4 mol · kg^-1) [44], lowering FAC of the carbon steel outlet feeder pipes that carry coolant from the reactor to the steam generators.

Film-forming substances, additives containing surface-active compounds that adsorb on metals and oxides to create protective films (see also Section 3.2), are increasingly accepted for controlling corrosion and oxide transport in power plants. Their benefits have been known for decades, but bad experiences with haphazard dosing and overdosing kept them largely ignored until recently. IAPWS has now published a technical guidance document (TGD) [45] on their use in fossil plants, application to nuclear plants has been considered [46], their properties and use have been reviewed [47], and two IAPWS international conferences on the topic took place in Lucerne, Switzerland (2017) and Prague, Czech Republic (2018). Practical plant aspects are covered in a later section.

Film-forming substances are conveniently split into film-forming amine products (FFAP), which contain film-forming amines (FFA) and are more common, and other film-forming products (FFP), which use non-amine surface-active substances whose identities are usually proprietary. FFAs are long-chain organic molecules bearing one or more amine groups, for example octadecylamine (ODA), oleylamine (OLA) and oleylpropane diamine (OLDA). The nitrogen lone-pair electrons bind strongly to surfaces while the aliphatic chains extend into the fluid (Figure 7). Components treated with FFAs show hydrophobic surfaces when opened, meaning the organic film persists even after drying. Commercial FFAPs frequently also include alkalizing agents such as ammonia or cyclohexylamine (CHA) to give feedwater systems added protection by raising pH.

Laboratory work has shown FAC falling directly once an FFAP reaches the corroding surface. In one test, an on-line carbon steel probe in a 140 °C loop with practically no dissolved oxygen recorded FAC through chemistry changes [48]. At neutral pH25°C, wall thinning ran at 6.0 mm per year until the commercial product Cetamine® V219 (containing the FFA OLDA plus the alkalizing agent CHA) was added to about ~ 0.8 mg · kg^-1 FFA. As Figure 8 shows, pH25°C rose at once to 9.2 and the FAC rate (slope of wall thickness) dropped to 0.35 mm per year. Over the following eleven days the FFA concentration fell to an apparent equilibrium of 0.4 mg · kg^-1 through adsorption on loop surfaces, while pH25°C and FAC rate stayed constant. On day 17, ion exchange (IX) was brought in to return pH25°C to neutral, removing FFA from the bulk water; the FAC rate rose to 2.0 mm per year, showing residual protection of the probe. That protection vanished after five days, with the rate spontaneously doubling, and dosing CHA alone back to pH25°C 9.2 brought the rate down only to 0.82 mm per year, well above the value seen with the FFAP.

The experiment showed that the FFAP outperformed CHA alone at equal pH25°C, that some surface protection lasted several days after FFA left the bulk water, and it suggested that the adsorbed FFA was more than a monolayer. Fitting a simple first-order adsorption-desorption model to FFA concentrations measured after addition and removal gave kinetic constants [49] consistent with other literature values [50]. Later work found that Cetamine® G851, essentially the same FFA (OLDA) as Cetamine® V219 but without CHA, was also effective in the same feedwater conditions [51,52]. Probe surfaces after FFA exposure were generally hydrophobic and gave very broad laser-Raman absorption spectra, indicating FFA coverage. Hydrophobicity, judged from the shape of applied water drops, persisted on dried specimens for many weeks and months, but many drops applied quickly wetted the surface and removed it, after which it reappeared upon drying [53]; this contradicts the notion that the FFA film works by completely keeping water off the surface.

Laboratory tests in two-phase steam-water flow, in contrast, have found no FAC mitigation by film-forming substances beyond the effect of any alkalizing agent present. In a loop at 200 °C with steam voidages up to 97 %, Cetamine® V219 reduced on-line probe FAC rates only as much as its CHA content [48], and the exposed probes showed no signs of an FFA film (no hydrophobicity or broad Raman absorption), while loop surfaces wetted by fully condensed single-phase water downstream were hydrophobic. Proposed reasons for the poor two-phase performance were the high shear stress imposed by the fast two-phase fluid on the probe and the relative volatility of the FFA in the product [48]; the authors note that the two-phase flow was produced by throttling single-phase water, which still seems to have given equilibrium conditions at the specimens [54]. Likewise, a study of where FFA ends up around an operating plant detected none on evaporator or high-pressure turbine surfaces [55], although hydrophobic surfaces appear downstream in the LP turbine and condenser, and clear benefits have been seen in two-phase locations of air-cooled condensers (Section 4.7).

Alloying elements such as chromium, copper and molybdenum in carbon steel have long been known to change FAC rates [56], chromium especially lowering them greatly [18,57]; CANDU primary coolant outlet feeders made of carbon steel must now contain a minimum chromium level. Replacing SA 106 Grade B steel with 0.019 % Cr by SA 106 Grade C with 0.33 % Cr has cut CANDU feeder FAC rates by about 50 % [44]. A 1998 model of the chromium effect at different exposure times assumed that reducing chromium below 0.04 % Cr had no further effect and that the benefit grows with exposure time (Figure 9), but later laboratory tests demonstrated a distinct influence of chromium between 0.019 and 0.001 % Cr (Figure 10), so any lower limit must lie below 0.019 % Cr.

How chromium reduces FAC is still not fully clear. Since on-line probes able to track FAC continuously became available, experiments such as those behind Figure 10 have shown [22] that a constant, chromium-dependent FAC rate is set up quickly once steel meets the water, stays constant under fixed conditions over exposures of many days to several weeks, and that 0.001 % Cr and 0.019 % Cr steels exposed for similar times carry similar chromium levels in their oxide films. Different oxide dissolution rates alone cannot explain all of this (chromium-based oxides are fairly insoluble under reducing conditions, so chromium stays in the magnetite as iron dissolves). A model assuming that a chromium-based diffusion barrier forms at once on exposure, resembling a less protective form of the barrier on freshly exposed stainless steel that corrodes slowly from the start, with oxide dissolution and chromium enrichment of the bulk oxide continuing as before, has predicted FAC rates of steels with differing chromium contents rather well [58]. The authors regard it as a useful hypothesis until such a barrier is confirmed by detailed experiments or direct analysis of oxidized metal.

FAC proceeds readily when the chemistry is reducing; dosing oxygen into the process water instead lifts the surface potential and upsets the electrochemical reactions. As explained in Section 3, the water treatment recommended for fossil and combined-cycle/HRSG plants whose feedwater and evaporator materials are compatible relies on oxidizing conditions for minimum FAC [18,24]. For CANDUs, PWRs and other nuclear plants with steam generators, however, oxidizing conditions cannot be used because the steam generator tubing alloys are susceptible to localized corrosion.

The inhibiting action of oxygen is usually credited to the formation of the higher iron oxide haematite, α-Fe_2O_3, in place of the magnetite normally produced during FAC (Section 2.2). Haematite is a relatively insoluble ferric oxide with a typical red colour and is generally found on opened components where single-phase FAC has stopped. Maghaemite, γ-Fe_2O_3, frequently an intermediate when magnetite oxidizes to haematite, can also be present. Lepidocrocite, γ-FeOOH, another ferric oxide, may also appear, but because it is a common rust constituent it often forms when unprotected surfaces meet air and water after components are opened.

Ferric oxides need not form for FAC to be arrested or "stifled": oxygen added to a reducing system undergoing FAC would mainly take over from water as the oxidant while magnetite keeps forming, so the Schikorr reaction Eq. (5) is replaced by 6Fe(OH)_2 + O_2 = 2Fe_3O_4 + 6H_2O (7) (oxygen oxidizes ferrous hydroxide to magnetite and water). Alternatively, oxygen could take part in the M-O cathodic step, Eq. (2), replacing it with 2H_2O + O_2 + 4e^- = 4OH^- (8) (oxygen reduction to hydroxide ions). This would also halt hydrogen atom generation and any hydrogen effusion into the metal; as these reactions take place the surface potential rises and FAC stops.

Oxygen beyond that needed for these basic reactions would produce higher ferric oxides, and after stifling with the minimum oxygen, extended exposure would slowly convert magnetite to ferric oxides such as haematite, reddening surfaces: 2Fe_3O_4 + ½O_2 = 3Fe_2O_3 (9) (magnetite is oxidized to haematite). If fresh surfaces were always exposed to oxidizing conditions, ferric-based oxides would form from the start and FAC would not occur.

Oxygen stifling was investigated in a laboratory loop allowing precise control of conditions at the corroding surface. A steel with low chromium (0.001 % Cr) was monitored for FAC without interruption while oxygen was added to single-phase water in increasing steps, each lasting several days [59]. Under feedwater conditions (140 °C, ammonia to pH25°C 9.2, no reducing agent) with tubular on-line probes of two diameters giving two fluid velocities (Figure 11), FAC proceeded at a nearly steady rate until oxygen reached 1.12 to 1.22 µg · kg^-1, at which point FAC was stifled; in comparable runs with 100 µg · kg^-1 hydrazine, 1.8 to 2.9 µg · kg^-1 oxygen was needed [59]. The authors caution that in operating plants with large surface areas, much higher oxygen levels at the injection point would be needed to make all components sufficiently oxidizing.

When the experiment ended, the stifled probes were removed and their inner surfaces compared with those of probes that had kept corroding under similar conditions. SEM showed no difference in oxide film morphology between active and stifled probes, and confocal laser-Raman microscopy identified both oxides as magnetite with only occasional traces of haematite and lepidocrocite; the oxides were in fact typical of corroding probe surfaces from many FAC experiments, including oxygen-free ones.

Oxygen stifling is thought to be controlled by mass transfer of oxygen from the bulk water to the surface, so a higher FAC rate requires a larger oxygen flux. Woolsey [60] showed this by plotting oxygen concentration versus the FAC rate normalized by water density times the oxygen mass transfer coefficient for several FAC cases, obtaining a clear dividing line between arrested (stifled) and non-arrested FAC. The line slope should match the oxidation stoichiometry, but slopes found at 115 and 150 °C were lower than the 0.285 expected from Fe + ½O_2 + H_2O = Fe(OH)_2 (10) (iron, oxygen and water form ferrous hydroxide), which corresponds to Eq. (8) with all corroded iron converted to ferrous hydroxide.

Applying mass transfer theory to Figure 11, the oxygen mass transfer coefficients were 7.8 mm · s^-1 in the 1.6 mm probe and 3.7 mm · s^-1 in the 2.4 mm probe (derived with Ferrell and Himmelblau diffusivities [61] and the Berger and Hau correlation [62]). With measured stifling concentrations of 1.22 and 1.12 µg · kg^-1, the only relevant oxidation needing oxygen fluxes at such driving forces is the conversion of half of the corroded iron, as ferrous species, into magnetite. For the laboratory FAC rates of 0.6 and 0.3 mm per year, the stifling concentrations calculated from the stoichiometry of Eq. (7) are 0.99 and 1.06 µg · kg^-1, agreeing well with measurement.

The stifling reaction probably does not take place at the M-O, since the oxides were around 1 µm thick with low porosity (estimated by Sanchez-Caldera et al. as about 5.0 x 10^-4 [63], or about 0.1 in later work [64]); at the measured concentration the driving force is too small for oxygen to diffuse to the M-O for either porosity. Two possibilities remain: either the Fe(OH)_2 arriving through the oxide turns into magnetite and deposits at the O-S, reinforcing the diffusion barrier, or the dissolution step (Eq. (6)) is stopped.

Comparable laboratory tests under neutral conditions at 140 °C behaved differently: higher FAC rates were stifled only at higher oxygen levels (between 38 and 28 µg · kg^-1, Figure 12). The Figure 12 results can be explained without any oxide diffusion barrier, taking oxygen mass transfer coefficients of 4.6 mm · s^-1 for the 1.6 mm probe and 3.2 mm · s^-1 for the 2.4 mm probe, using 4Fe(OH)_2 + O_2 = 2Fe_2O_3 + 4H_2O (11) (ferrous hydroxide is oxidized directly to ferric oxide). Here all corroded iron arriving as ferrous species at the O-S, whether diffused through the oxide or dissolved, is converted at once to ferric species such as haematite, giving predicted stifling concentrations of 29.6 and 25.5 µg · kg^-1 for the 1.6 mm and 2.4 mm probes, close to the measured 38 and 28 µg · kg^-1.

Probes exposed to oxygen in neutral water showed higher ferric oxide concentrations than probes exposed at high pH [65]. This mechanistic contrast between neutral and pH25°C 9.2 conditions may reflect how pH affects ferrous oxidation, since lower pH25°C favours fully oxidized lepidocrocite and goethite, whereas magnetite forms in alkaline conditions [66]. Notably, in an FAC test with multiple tubular specimens in pH25°C 9.2 water at 140 °C, oxidizing conditions laid thick haematite layers over magnetite on one corroding specimen; as the micrograph of Figure 13 shows, the deposit apparently grew from upstream to downstream and stopped abruptly mid-probe, presumably by precipitation from a high dissolved iron concentration [54]. This represents another route to haematite on component surfaces and matches haematite observed in the low- and intermediate-pressure drums of HRSGs in combined-cycle plants.

Flow is critical for FAC (Figure 4), yet the dependence cannot simply be on bulk flow rate, because different parts of one pipe carrying the same fluid corrode at different FAC rates. Turbulence is evidently involved, since bends, constrictions, expansions and similar disturbances that raise turbulence show heavier attack. Figure 1 shows enhanced attack downstream of a constriction (ferrule) where turbulence effects should peak: the jet streamlines from the orifice reattach to the wall about two pipe diameters downstream, forming a recirculating eddy. CFD modelling of flow after an orifice routinely places maximum FAC near the reattachment point of the separated flow, where both wall shear stress and mass transfer are high.

Poulson [68] proposed that mass transfer profiles downstream of a sudden expansion are more likely than shear stress profiles to mirror FAC attack. Figure 14 gives normalized measured wall profiles of initially identical carbon steel tubes just downstream of a sudden expansion after 14 days in neutral water at 140 °C at different Reynolds numbers, and Figure 15 gives the matching Sherwood numbers for mass transfer computed with the ANSYS-CFX CFD code [69], obtained via the equivalent heat transfer parameters because ANSYS cannot compute mass transfer directly. Such modelling must recognize that as FAC proceeds the metal profile changes, moving the values and profiles of the flow parameters; allowing for this shifts and widens the computed Sherwood profile of Figure 15 into that of Figure 16, which also matches the measured damage profile of Figure 14.

Sh = km · d · DAB^-1 (Sherwood number = mass transfer coefficient km × initial tube diameter d ÷ mass diffusion coefficient DAB), used to express the computed mass transfer downstream of the expansion [69].

Wall shear stress and other flow parameter profiles likewise evolve with the damage profile. Figure 17 shows how the computed wall shear stress profile downstream of a sudden expansion in a tube corroding like those of Figure 14 moves as damage progresses: as with the mass transfer peak of Figure 16, the shear stress peak moves downstream, the profile flattens overall, and the theoretical minimum at the reattachment point is smeared along the tube by the damage. FAC rate has been reasonably correlated with computed static shear stress downstream of an orifice [70].

Mass transfer modelling has been carried out for pipe bends under CANDU primary coolant conditions, without considering evolving damage [71], and the computed patterns agreed spatially quite well with measured FAC damage. The conclusion was that FAC was mass transfer controlled and could be quantified as the local mass transfer coefficient multiplied by the ferrous ion concentration difference between the O-S and the bulk water. This view is shared by most papers on FAC mechanisms and underlies complex FAC prediction codes.

The authors argue, as before [22], that the mass transfer model is theoretically untenable because mass transfer is only the second step of the overall mechanism. The first step is dissolution, which regulates oxide thickness and generates at the O-S half of the ferrous ions that then cross the flow boundary layer into the bulk, while the remaining half come from the M-O by diffusing through the oxide (Eqs. (1), (4) and (5)). Berge [72] combined the two steps in series as FAC rate = kd km (Ceq – Cb)/(0.5km + kd) (11) (FAC rate from dissolution rate constant kd, mass transfer coefficient km, iron solubility Ceq at the exposure conditions and bulk iron concentration Cb).

Because flow plainly matters, the dissolution term of Eq. (11) was dropped (implying kd >> km), giving FAC rate = km ( Ceq – Cb ) (12) (FAC rate = mass transfer coefficient × difference between iron solubility and bulk iron concentration). This widely used expression is equivalent to the Pietralik formulation [71], since under mass transfer control the effective O-S concentration tends to Ceq, and it is the basis of FAC prediction codes such as Electricité de France's BRT-CICERO™ [73]. The authors stress that it is untenable because dissolution cannot be neglected, as recognized in 2002 [64] when early magnetite dissolution kinetics data under reactor primary coolant conditions [74] indicated kd << km for CANDU feeders. An alternative model was then developed in which dissolution loosens the oxide crystallites at the O-S, letting fluid forces detach them more easily, adding a further oxide thinning process [75].

Cross-section micrographs of oxide on steel that underwent FAC under reactor primary coolant conditions show an aggregated crystallite structure, supporting the plausibility of this mechanism (Figure 3). The model assumed that particle removal, by spalling or erosion, is driven by wall shear stress. Although fluid shear stresses have been noted to be too weak to remove oxide mechanically [76], crystallites loosened by dissolution might be removable by these weak forces, or removal may be helped by "freak" turbulence events that travel through the boundary layer and exert larger surface forces [75,77]. The apparent mismatch between shear stress profiles and FAC damage, especially downstream of disturbances where reattachment of separated flow creates a theoretical stagnation point [68], also hints that other forces dominate, although such arguments generally overlook the shift of profiles as FAC advances (Figure 17).

Because oxide dissolution is a primary FAC mechanism, it is relevant that computed shear stress profiles over magnetite disks dissolving under a submerged jet in laboratory tests at power plant conditions match the dissolution craters well. In Figure 18, for a 10 mm-diameter disk struck centrally by 140 °C, neutral pH25°C water from a 0.5 mm orifice, dissolution was lower near the central stagnation point [78]. The corresponding Table 2 entry shows dissolution was mainly dissolution-controlled with some mass transfer influence (crater-averaged dissolution rate constant 2.2 mm · s^-1 against an average mass transfer coefficient of 13.9 mm · s^-1). Unlike the reattachment point behind a pipe constriction, the stagnation point in these centro-symmetric jet tests evidently stayed put as the surface profile evolved.

Mass transfer coefficients in power plant circuits usually lie between about 2 and 20 mm · s^-1, but they are generally estimated from correlations derived under less demanding conditions and are uncertain; for instance, the Mihama-3 PWR pipe downstream of the orifice where rupture occurred was separately estimated at 3 mm · s^-1 [80] and at 30 mm · s^-1 [81]. Simply inserting Table 2 kd values into models such as Berge et al. [72] implies that, in the alkaline conditions typical of feedwater and nuclear primary coolant, FAC is governed by dissolution kinetics with little flow effect, which is clearly untenable. Under neutral chemistry, however, mass transfer does matter, as the experiments of Figure 10 show.

Magnetite dissolution in FAC is electrochemical: being reductive (Eq. (6)) and involving electron transfer, it depends on the surface potential reached during corrosion. Modelling [64,82] suggests the potential might increase kd by as much as tenfold depending on conditions, while still leaving dissolution apparently in control under the Berge model [72]. Table 2 implies some mass transfer influence under neutral conditions at low Sherwood numbers, consistent with the nearly linear dependence of FAC on km in the neutral experiments of Figure 10, whereas the very strong flow dependence seen in comparable alkaline experiments was probably due to crystallite erosion [22].

Another consideration for simple Berge-type models is that the effective iron saturation concentration under plant conditions (Ceq in Eq. (12)) is itself a function of the corroding surface's electrochemical potential. In CANDU primary coolant FAC, the corrosion potential of the steel has been reported [83,84] as –0.75 to –1.0 V versus the saturated hydrogen electrode (SHE). In early FAC modelling [64], including this electrochemical effect in equilibrium solubility changed Ceq by a factor of 5 to 11 depending on circuit location. A complete description of FAC should combine the electrochemistry of corrosion, oxide growth and dissolution with the relevant fluid dynamics and coolant redox reactions, as in the extensive Japanese-led studies, particularly for nuclear systems [85].

Wet steam systems in power plants, such as feedwater heater drains, HRSGs, deaerators, air-cooled condensers and LP turbines, are susceptible to two-phase FAC (Section 4); only wetted surfaces are attacked and damage is frequently severe. The vapour phase affects how well FAC control additives such as amines work: ammonia partitions into steam in power plant systems, cyclohexylamine behaves similarly, and ethanolamine (ETA) favours the liquid phase [54]. Oxygen brings little benefit in two-phase systems. Volatility together with basicity are therefore key selection criteria for an FAC control additive, discussed further later.

At low steam qualities FAC behaves like single-phase attack, so the mechanisms above dominate; CANDU pressurized heavy-water reactor outlet feeders with primary-coolant FAC classed as single-phase often had steam voidages of up to 20 %. Single-phase behaviour is expected where liquid is the main phase and steam is present as bubbles, developing into slugs and then into annular flow with entrained droplets and liquid films as quality increases. High qualities give thin liquid films around fast vapour cores with entrained droplets, and the film may break into patches or rivulets, so that FAC becomes affected by mechanical effects like liquid droplet impingement and mechanical erosion.

If the fluid characteristics of low quality flows are known, FAC can be modelled with the single-phase mechanisms of Section 2.5: wall mass transfer and shear stress for steam-water flow in a tube are obtained from standard correlations and estimated friction coefficients of each phase, based on fluid properties and phase Reynolds numbers. Knowing the liquid chemistry relative to the vapour and the steel susceptibility (for example its chromium content), these inputs can be fed into a single-phase model to estimate FAC. Figure 19 sets model predictions against FAC measured in test tubes in a 200 °C laboratory loop, using several amines at pH25°C 9.2 and a range of steam voidages [86].

Harsher conditions at high steam qualities raise FAC rates and give irregular damage patterns, such as "tiger striping" where the corroding film flows as rivulets, or "shot-gun" damage where entrained droplets strike at high velocity. The latter, liquid droplet impingement (LDI), often looks like cavitation erosion/corrosion and occurs in air vent lines and feedwater heaters of steam raising plant. LDI is commonly split into LDI corrosion and LDI erosion [87]: LDI corrosion resembles aggravated single-phase FAC governed by chemistry, metal properties, droplet size and collision velocity set by the overall flow pattern.

LDI erosion has been described empirically as log(R) = 4.8log(vr) – log(Ne) – 16.65 + 0.67log(dp) – 0.22K (13) (R, the volumetric metal loss per volume of liquid impinged, as a function of droplet collision velocity vr, erosion resistance number Ne, droplet diameter dp and geometry factor K). Ne [88] depends on the metal's mechanical properties and allows comparison between metals, and K ranges from 0 for a plane surface to 1 for a curved one. Okada et al. [87] report significant LDI wall thinning at steam velocities above 200 m · s^-1 with steam qualities of 95 % to 99.8 % and droplet diameters of 5 to 100 µm.

FAC normally produces scalloping, a characteristic sculpted or dimpled surface with a cuspate texture; many industrial examples appear in Section 4.7. Figure 20 is an SEM image of scalloping in CANDU outlet feeder pipes made of low chromium (0.019 % Cr) steel and cooled by heavy water (the apparent pH here, adjusted with lithium oxide, is the room-temperature reading of the D_2O solution with an electrode calibrated in H_2O). At primary coolant temperatures, unlike feedwater temperatures, magnetite solubility rises with pH25°C (Figure 6), so greater alkalinity increases FAC. The scallops are roughly 0.5–0.75 mm wide and 0.2 mm deep with a magnetite film averaging 0.8 µm, and the mean corrosion rate over the 14-year exposure was 110 µm per year [64].

Scalloping also has natural analogues. Fast streams sculpt river beds and caves into scalloped forms much larger than FAC scallops in pipes, attributed to uneven rock dissolution by the adjacent turbulent water [90]. Hollows and grooves on melting ice have been linked to cellular vortices in the air above [91], turbulent air can scallop snow fields, and the scalloped Antarctic snow field of Figure 21 strongly resembles the feeder pipe surface of Figure 20.

Much thinking on scallop development, including whether scallops start from surface defects or arise purely from fluid dynamics, comes from experiments with water flowing over plaster of Paris. Allen [90] cut defects into flat plaster surfaces in a rectangular channel and observed them grow over time into "flutes" (resembling heel prints) and "grooves" (narrow flutes); without artificial initiation they arose from natural plaster defects and, as more formed, merged into scallop patterns. Hydrodynamic work of that period introduced a scallop Reynolds number of 23 000 based on average scallop size [93]. Later comparison of pure plaster tubes with sand-seeded plaster under the same dissolution conditions [94] concluded that defects are needed for scallops to form.

Modelling of scallop effects on FAC has mostly focused on enhanced mass transfer [95,96], usually derived from the classic pressure drop analogy treating scallops as relative wall roughness. This is a simplification: the natural scallop shape gives a larger pressure drop for flow opposite to the direction that formed them than for flow in that direction, and the latter case produces pressure drops that classic relative roughness concepts cannot model realistically [97].

Early observations of FAC scallops in reactor outlet piping (Figure 20) led to the view [98] that fluid dynamics alone set the corrosion pattern and metal properties hardly mattered. Comparing industrial pipes with small laboratory tubes is instructive: Figure 22 shows a low chromium (0.001 % Cr) carbon steel tube after 184 days of FAC under feedwater conditions (pH25°C 9.2 with ammonia, 140 °C), whose bore widened from 2.4 mm to 3.2 mm, equivalent to 0.8 mm per year on average. Its scallops, produced at a mean pipe Reynolds number of 6.0 x 10^4, average ~ 0.7 mm, giving a scallop Reynolds number of 19 000, whereas the Figure 20 reactor pipe, at Reynolds number 8.0 x 10^6, gives 63 000. A universal scallop Reynolds number therefore clearly does not hold for such FAC cases.

The final scallop pattern probably results from the turbulence scale combined with inhomogeneities of the metal surface. These inhomogeneities affect oxide structure, which grows differently on different grains and over pearlite can stand up to about a micrometre above the oxide on neighbouring ferrite, as the higher magnification views of Figure 22 show. Figure 23 likewise shows at high magnification the irregular magnetite profile on a specimen exposed for 28 days to neutral 140 °C water with < 10 µg · kg^-1 dissolved oxygen (average FAC rate 4.8 mm per year), with coral-like protruding magnetite over the pearlite grains.

As the corroding surface recedes, oxide structures disturb the flow and start new scallops, some of which grow while others are erased, implying that for a given turbulence regime a finer metal grain structure gives more scallops; the cross-section micrographs of Figure 24 show the finer pearlite of the Figure 20 steel compared with the Figure 22 steel. Kolmogorov turbulence theory [99] further indicates that eddies at the smallest scale in the large, high-Reynolds-number pipe are roughly half as big as in the small, low-Reynolds-number tube (in both, the smallest-to-largest eddy ratio is roughly Re^-0.75). The tube, with lower Reynolds number and coarser pearlite, should thus form larger scallops than the industrial pipe, as observed. Also, higher-turbulence regions of one component, such as downstream of an orifice or at an elbow extrados, show higher FAC rates and smaller scallops [100,101], again matching smaller local eddies.

In two-phase steam-water flows, for example wet steam lines, feedwater heater drains and deaerator-separator equipment, scallops look locally much like those in single-phase equipment (see Section 4.7 for fossil and combined-cycle/HRSG scalloping). Because FAC attacks only water-touched surfaces and the water-steam distribution depends on local geometry, steam quality and bulk flow, overall FAC patterns differ from place to place, though single-phase mechanisms still apply inside the liquid film. Local chemistry therefore matters as well as fluid dynamics: with all-volatile treatment (AVT), the pH-raising component may move into the steam and leave the liquid relatively corrosive, and oxidizing environments and oxygenated treatment fail in two-phase regions for the same reason. Opened equipment often shows FAC areas next to uncorroded areas, presumably because liquid tends to channel into an established FAC region and intensify attack; tiger-striping is a severe case.

A number of computer codes, mostly for nuclear systems, have been written to manage FAC and give operators information for minimizing damage risk to piping and components. Essentially they manage data: they take wall thickness measurements from prescribed monitoring of pipework and components and flag vulnerable areas. Any prediction they offer is in the end empirical, relying on fitted functions for material, flow and chemistry effects that are adjusted as plant data arrive; interpolation and extrapolation of ultrasonic testing results, for instance, indicate conditions in uninspected areas and the risk of excessive damage. Even a mechanistic model (Section 2.5) has parameters tuned to match measurements. The main codes are described in detail elsewhere [28], so only short descriptions with comments are given here.

Checworks®, together with derivative Chec codes such as Checmate®, is the most widely used software internationally; it was developed by the Electric Power Research Institute (US), and its principles are embodied in a fossil plant version, the Fossil FAC Advisor®. Its algorithm multiplies together factors representing temperature, mass transfer, geometry, pH, oxygen level, alloy composition and steam quality to obtain the FAC rate. Although it claims to be based on the Berge model [72], it neglects magnetite dissolution kinetics, an anomaly (Section 2.5) presumably compensated by tuning the factors during validation against plant and laboratory data. Users build a plant model from design parameters and heat balances and enter current operating conditions, component materials and geometry (size and wall thickness), replacement history and inspection data; the software then forecasts FAC rates and remaining wall thickness in susceptible lines, checks these against inspection results and gives the time to critical thickness. The Checworks Owners Group (CHUG) has warned of heavier attack just downstream of a component of more resistant material, where the boundary layer is low in dissolved iron and hence more corrosive (the entrance effect [102], distinct from, though interacting with, the hydraulic boundary layer entrance effect).

Electricité de France (EDF) built the BRT-CICERO® code from mechanistic principles on the Berge model [72], again omitting oxide dissolution kinetics and so carrying the anomaly of Section 2.5; mass transfer becomes controlling and is computed from a standard straight-pipe correlation adjusted for other geometries by an empirical factor, with the mass transfer relations confirmed in many loop experiments. For piping elements, scalloping is represented by a fixed roughness height of 40 µm (see Section 2.7). Material effects enter as factors of chromium, molybdenum and copper concentrations raised to powers below one; chromium dominates but is assigned a threshold as in Figure 9, an assumption criticized in Section 2.2. Oxygen affects single-phase FAC according to its access to surfaces via the mass transfer coefficient, assuming haematite rather than magnetite formation (Section 2.3), with a threshold of 7 to 15 µg · kg^-1 taken from high temperature loop tests.

With growing BRT-CICERO® experience across French plants and a very large database, a probabilistic treatment of measurements has been introduced to make predictions more reliable and to optimize inspection and maintenance frequency. Inputs include pipe thicknesses measured on prescribed grids, chromium content, thermalhydraulic conditions and geometry of each component, and operating chemistry over the cycle. The program identifies high risk areas for thinning and has successfully indicated severe damage, though it appears highly conservative for some components [103].

Following the 1986 Surry PWR accident, KWU/Siemens-AG in Germany produced the WATHEC code for analysing inspection data and helping operators avoid further piping damage [104]; it covers both two-phase steam-water and single-phase water flows. Empirical links between wall loss and operating variables (flow rate, temperature, material composition, pH) were derived in an extensive early laboratory programme at the AREVA test facilities, with geometry factors for bends, tees, constrictions and the like. Two-phase flow is handled by applying the relations to the liquid film, allowing for the distribution of alkalizing agents and oxygen between liquid and vapour, and the relations were continually refined with plant data. The code picks out susceptible pipe lengths, then specific likely high-FAC spots from flow and geometry, and its predictive model estimates thinning and evaluates it against the plant database. Since 1998 it has been extended and incorporated in the COMSY system for component aging and plant life management in general; COMSY users provide a model of the plant system with thermalhydraulic parameters, material compositions and chemistry, while in-depth analyses need component data such as manufacturing tolerances and yield stress and are usually shown as lifetime evolution charts.

Russia's RAMEK code, developed in the late 1980s, covers FAC in both single-phase water and two-phase steam-water systems and treats their mechanisms as substantially different [105]; the authors note, however, that attack on magnetite inside the liquid film of wet steam or low quality flow looks the same as in single-phase flow provided the flow characteristics and the liquid/vapour split of additives and dissolved gases are accounted for. Steam-water flow is treated as more aggressive, with high shear stresses and droplet impingement eroding the surfaces mechanically. The regime governed by removal of dissolved iron combines a conventional convective mass transfer coefficient with a coefficient for extra turbulence from local "freak" events such as the turbulent bursts of Section 2.5, the two coefficients being summed in a rate expression equivalent to Eq. (12). The other regime, removal of particulate oxide, is taken as proportional to a combination of mean wall shear stress and an extreme shear stress value. The two regime expressions are additive, and their constants, which depend on material properties and system thermalhydraulics and chemistry, came from an extensive laboratory programme.

RAMEK is routinely used to estimate component piping FAC and predict maximum attack locations; it includes a database of plant systems listing susceptible areas and their measured FAC and is frequently used to plan inspection programmes and maintenance schedules. According to Betova et al. [28], a later code family, the ECI series and ECI-DS, has been qualified for water-water energetic reactor (VVER) units; no details are available, but they seem to follow the same mechanistic principles as RAMEK, and the ECI-01 version is reported to be generally conservative in predicting pipe wall loss.

Overall, recent information and analyses show that the basic mechanisms underpinning several commercial codes are flawed, which may explain the differing predictive abilities revealed by the recent IAEA international benchmarking study [21], where only "fair" agreement among codes was ascribed to differences in theory and models [106]. Even so, the empirical fitting to measurements and continual adjustment as databases grow seem adequate for acceptable predictions of FAC degradation within individual plants, and at minimum, their ability to pinpoint high risk areas and manage data makes the codes valuable to operators.

Figure 25 gives a simple scheme of the FAC mechanism discussed in Section 2, showing the reactions and transport steps inside the oxide film in a reducing environment; it equals the pores-solution model of general carbon steel corrosion in iron-saturated or near-saturated solutions, except that dissolution at the oxide-solution surface replaces precipitation of an outer layer. Protection comes from the oxide film, which governs the diffusion processes. In the simplest picture water reaches the metal easily; the anodic reaction yields ferrous ions and the balancing cathodic reaction yields hydrogen atoms ("nascent hydrogen") and hydroxyl ions. At ~ 300 °C all hydrogen atoms effuse through the metal (x = 12 in Figure 25), while at lower temperatures some combine into molecules that pass through the oxide toward the bulk fluid.

At the metal-oxide interface, ferrous and hydroxyl ions form dissolved ferrous hydroxide; half of it decomposes oxidatively to magnetite that fills the volume of reacted metal and releases hydrogen molecules that diffuse toward the fluid, while the other half diffuses through the oxide into the bulk fluid (in ordinary corrosion it would precipitate as outer-layer magnetite). At the O-S, magnetite dissolves reductively to ferrous hydroxide, at steady state using exactly the hydrogen generated by its formation at the M-O. Anything that speeds dissolution, chemically by raising magnetite solubility and dissolution kinetics or hydrodynamically by raising mass transfer and removal of dissolved iron, thins the oxide and accelerates transport, increasing corrosion and magnetite formation at the M-O until a new steady state is reached; thinner oxide means faster FAC.

Oxide films in single-phase feedwater systems are typically up to about a micrometre thick, but in two-phase conditions below ~ 150 °C they may be only a fraction of that and can appear as interference films when coherent enough. At steady state in Figure 25, six iron atoms corroded at the M-O are balanced by six ferrous hydroxide molecules released at the O-S and transported across the flow boundary layer by mass transfer. Greater turbulence thins this boundary layer and raises mass transfer, increasing oxide dissolution and FAC rate, and dissolution can also promote erosion or removal of oxide particles by fluid forces.

Fluid chemistry acts on FAC through oxide dissolution. Under feedwater conditions magnetite dissolution rate and solubility peak at ~ 140 °C and fall with rising pH (Figure 5), so an alkalizing agent is dosed to minimize FAC. In nuclear primary coolant, solubility rises with pH25°C above ~ 10 and with temperature above ~ 300 °C, so alkalinity is held at the low end of the permitted range. In both cases the magnetite dissolution rate constant is below the mass transfer coefficient, so the basic pores-solution model would be dissolution-controlled and predict no flow effect; to resolve this, modelling has quantified particulate erosion driven by fluid-dynamic forces and assisted by dissolution, an additional oxide-thinning process that has given good predictions of observed FAC rates. When dissolved oxygen makes the Figure 25 system sufficiently oxidizing, magnetite forms without hydrogen and dissolution at the O-S ceases, stifling FAC; long oxygen exposure tends to transform magnetite into ferric oxides such as practically insoluble haematite and lepidocrocite.

paragraphs.section: 3 Cycle Chemistry Aspects of Controlling FAC
paragraphs.text: Section 2 showed that in every generating system FAC is dictated by the cycle chemistry in use, and, as later shown, poorly optimized chemistry controls and procedures most commonly cause FAC in fossil and combined-cycle/HRSG plants. Nuclear feedwater systems are operated mainly to protect the reactor (direct-cycle plants) or the steam generator (SG) (dual-cycle plants), largely by controlling corrosion product transport. BWRs limit ingress to the reactor mainly through high-efficiency filtration and condensate polishing, whereas dual-cycle reactors protect SGs by chemistry: high pH reduces FAC and corrosion product ingress, and reducing conditions limit stress corrosion cracking (SCC) risk. Because reducing conditions tend to promote carbon steel FAC, plants with vulnerable materials must optimize chemistry, and regular inspection of pipe wall thinning is essential, since the Table 1 incidents occurred in poorly monitored areas.

paragraphs.section: 3 Cycle Chemistry Aspects of Controlling FAC
paragraphs.text: This part does not attempt a full treatise on power plant cycle chemistry; it covers documented chemistry control principles for mitigating FAC. Nuclear plant chemistry is usually specified by the reactor vendor and supplemented by R&D recommendations from industry bodies such as EPRI (US), VGB PowerTech (Germany) and EDF for light water reactors; for the Canadian PHWRs this role falls to the CANDU Owners Group (COG). Control scheme details are generally not public [107,108], but the broadly similar principles are often published in papers and proceedings [109]; their FAC relevance is summarized below. For fossil and combined-cycle/HRSG plants, short outlines of the latest IAPWS-recommended chemistries for FAC control follow [23-26,45,110].

paragraphs.section: 3.1 Cycle Chemistry Treatments for Fossil and Combined-Cycle Plants
paragraphs.text: The condensate/feedwater pH is usually raised by dosing a volatile alkalizing agent, typically ammonia, or alternatively an alkalizing amine. Recently some plants have used film-forming substances (FFS) instead of ammonia or alkalizing amine to help tackle FAC [45]. The FFS family includes film-forming amines (FFA), film-forming amine products (FFAP) and film-forming products without amines (FFP); they are normally proprietary with compositions unknown to users and are mostly supplied blended with an alkalizing amine, in which case they are called film-forming amine products. Considerable international work is under way to produce guidance confirming their ability to reduce FAC (see Section 2.2).

paragraphs.section: 3.1 Cycle Chemistry Treatments for Fossil and Combined-Cycle Plants
paragraphs.text: Three volatile treatments are commonly applied to condensate and feedwater in fossil plants and to condensate, feedwater and evaporator water in combined-cycle/HRSG plants; since they are defined and controlled by oxidation-reduction potential (ORP), this parameter is explained first [111]. ORP is the same as the redox potential used widely in electrochemistry and corrosion science and must not be confused with corrosion potential, although it is a useful indicator of environmental corrosivity: ORP expresses the oxidizing/reducing power of the environment, while corrosion potential reflects the corrosion reaction on the metal surface, and the two generally track each other without being equal.

paragraphs.section: 3.1 Cycle Chemistry Treatments for Fossil and Combined-Cycle Plants
paragraphs.text: ORP can be a very good tool for controlling fossil feedwater chemistry, corrosion and FAC, but readings must be interpreted carefully because ORP varies with pH25°C, dissolved oxygen partial pressure, mass transport properties, flow rates and cycle materials. ORP values are therefore not directly comparable between units, similar units with similar oxygen and/or reducing agent levels may read differently because of measuring differences, and the redox neutral potential at which conditions switch from reducing to oxidizing is not fixed. ORP can nonetheless control the oxidizing power of feedwater in all-ferrous systems or the reducing power in mixed-metallurgy systems; the former is seldom done, but the latter is the essential control for mixed-metallurgy feedwater systems [24].

paragraphs.section: 3.1 Cycle Chemistry Treatments for Fossil and Combined-Cycle Plants
paragraphs.text: AVT(R) – All-Volatile Treatment (Reducing) [24]: condensate or feedwater receives ammonia, an amine, an FFS or an amine blend of lower volatility than ammonia, plus a reducing agent (usually hydrazine or an accepted substitute such as carbohydrazide). When air in-leakage keeps condensate oxygen fairly low, at roughly 10 µg · kg^-1 or below (normally measured at the condensate pump discharge, CPD), the feedwater acquires a reducing ORP; higher oxygen (> 20 µg · kg^-1) from heavy air in-leakage usually prevents a reducing environment yet is often wrongly met by overdosing reducing agent. AVT(R) protects copper-based alloys in mixed-metallurgy fossil feedwater systems but should not be used in multi-pressure HRSGs because of single-phase FAC (Section 2). Hence a basic international rule prohibits reducing agents both in combined-cycle/HRSG plants and in fossil plants whose feedwater systems are all-ferrous, to prevent single-phase FAC [24].

paragraphs.section: 3.1 Cycle Chemistry Treatments for Fossil and Combined-Cycle Plants
paragraphs.text: AVT(O) – All-Volatile Treatment (Oxidizing) [24]: over the last 25 years this has become the strongly preferred treatment for fossil feedwater systems containing only all-ferrous materials (the condenser may still contain copper alloys) [112] and for combined-cycle/HRSG plants; in these, no reducing agent should be used during operation or shutdown/layup. Dosing of ammonia, an amine, an FFS or a lower-volatility amine blend takes place at the CPD or at the condensate polisher outlet where a polisher exists. Multi-pressure combined-cycle/HRSG plants lacking feedwater copper alloys should use this treatment, and with reasonably good air in-leakage control (oxygen 10–20 µg · kg^-1) the feedwater ORP is mildly oxidizing.

paragraphs.section: 3.1 Cycle Chemistry Treatments for Fossil and Combined-Cycle Plants
paragraphs.text: OT – Oxygenated Treatment [24]: in conventional fossil plants, optimized OT uses one oxygen injection point at the condensate polisher outlet (CPO), with feedwater heater and deaerator vents closed and ammonia also dosed at the CPO. A minimum oxygen level is often needed to fully passivate, and keep passivated, the single-phase flow regions of the main feedwater line and drain lines: usually 30 to 50 µg · kg^-1 at the economizer inlet for drum units (set according to the boiler recirculation ratio) and 30–150 µg · kg^-1 for once-through/supercritical units. OT is far less common in combined-cycle/HRSG plants, but AVT(O) with low oxygen (< 10 µg · kg^-1) frequently lacks the oxidizing power to passivate the huge internal surfaces of the preheaters, the LP, intermediate-pressure (IP) and high-pressure (HP) economizers, and the LP evaporators, particularly with a deaerator in the LP circuit, in which case oxygen can be dosed at conventional recirculating cycle levels. OT is the feedwater choice for fossil units with all-ferrous feedwater heaters, a condensate polisher and the ability to keep conductivity after cation exchange (CACE) < 0.15 µS · cm^-1 under all operating conditions.

paragraphs.section: 3.1 Cycle Chemistry Treatments for Fossil and Combined-Cycle Plants
paragraphs.text: In HRSGs of combined-cycle plants, boiler water treatment is commonly used to prevent FAC in LP and IP evaporators and economizer circuits, using one of two non-volatile alkalizing agents, tri-sodium phosphate for phosphate treatment (PT) or sodium hydroxide for caustic treatment (CT) [25]. PT – Phosphate Treatment [25]: phosphate chemicals have served as the most common boiler/HRSG evaporator treatments worldwide, but a historical variety of phosphate compounds and blends with other philosophies produced widely differing control limits for pH, phosphate level and sodium-to-phosphate molar ratio, along with reliability problems. Over more than 25 years, consolidated worldwide experience shows that tri-sodium phosphate (TSP) alone should be dosed, within limits set by a 3:1 sodium-to-phosphate molar ratio, 1 mg · kg^-1 TSP (with 0.3 mg · kg^-1 as the minimum) and NaOH to keep pH25°C above 9.0; this excludes mono- and/or di-sodium phosphate and so removes the possibility of acid phosphate corrosion. The 0.3 mg · kg^-1 value is only a minimum, and protection improves with phosphate as high as possible without breaching steam sodium limits.

paragraphs.section: 3.1 Cycle Chemistry Treatments for Fossil and Combined-Cycle Plants
paragraphs.text: CT – Caustic Treatment [25]: In HRSG drum-type boilers, CT is an option for reducing FAC risk where all-volatile treatment has been ineffective, or where PT has been unsatisfactory because of hideout or monitoring and control problems. Sodium hydroxide dosing to boiler/evaporator water must be closely controlled to limit caustic carryover into steam, which could cause stress corrosion cracking damage in steam circuits and turbines.

paragraphs.section: 3.1 Cycle Chemistry Treatments for Fossil and Combined-Cycle Plants
paragraphs.text: FFSs – Film-Forming Substances [45]: use of FFS in fossil and combined-cycle/HRSG plants is growing worldwide and has lowered FAC rates in these plants and in air-cooled condensers, as discussed later. As noted in Section 2.2, FFSs act differently from conventional treatments by adsorbing on metal and metal oxide/deposit surfaces and forming a molecular or multi-molecular physical barrier between the water/water-steam and the surface, evidenced by hydrophobic surfaces of drained components. The three main active substances used historically are ODA, OLA and OLDA, and commercial FFS formulations often add alkalizing amines, emulsifiers, reducing agents and dispersants such as polycarboxylates. Much confusion exists about their use in normal operation and shutdown/layup, and until a recent IAPWS document [45] there was no international guidance to help decide if an FFS should be used and if the plant would gain from it. An FFS must be tailored to each plant after an extensive cycle chemistry review and is dosed at the CPD or polisher outlet; more and more reports indicate that FFSs give single-phase and, in some plant areas, two-phase FAC protection (Section 2.2).

paragraphs.section: 3.2 Cycle Chemistry Treatments for Nuclear Plants
paragraphs.text: A priority of nuclear plant chemistry control is minimizing corrosion product generation and transport in the feedwater system. In BWRs, corrosion products go straight into the reactor and can impair fuel performance, so their transport is limited by condensate polishing and high performance filtration. In dual-cycle reactors, corrosion products foul SG tubes and reduce efficiency while also harbouring and concentrating aggressive impurities, and their ingress is controlled mainly by chemistry. In 2017 there were reportedly [113] 1281 steam generators in operation in water-cooled reactors worldwide and 193 under construction. PWRs are tubed with Incoloy (Alloy 800) or Inconel (Alloy 600 and Alloy 690), VVERs use austenitic stainless steel (later models nickel alloy), and PHWRs use Alloy 800, Alloy 600 and Monel (Alloy 400).

paragraphs.section: 3.2 Cycle Chemistry Treatments for Nuclear Plants
paragraphs.text: Much early FAC research was done in the United Kingdom [41] for the advanced gas-cooled reactor (AGR): 14 reactors, each having as many as 12 boilers (steam generators) whose tubing changes alloy along the path because the primary gas is so hot: the economizer is carbon steel, the evaporator ferritic Fe9Cr1Mo steel and the secondary superheater austenitic AISI type 316 stainless steel. SG alloys are shielded from localized corrosion, chiefly SCC, by cycle chemistry that keeps conditions reducing (low electrochemical corrosion potential (ECP)), whereas high pH, supplemented in a few cases by oxygen injection, keeps FAC and corrosion product formation down. Because reducible oxides like haematite, goethite, lepidocrocite and copper oxides can increase ECP, so their ingress and formation, for instance during shutdown and layup, should be avoided, and keeping pH high during maintenance outages favours magnetite over ferric species [66].

paragraphs.section: 3.2 Cycle Chemistry Treatments for Nuclear Plants
paragraphs.text: AVT, similar to the fossil plant treatment described above and exemplified by its use in PWRs [109], is now the preferred secondary cycle treatment for nuclear plants. The wide variety of materials and local conditions means no single chemistry programme suits every plant, even of nominally identical design [107], but general principles hold industry-wide, and commercial software such as ChemWorksTM guides plant-specific chemistry control. After phosphate treatment was largely replaced by ammonia in the 1970s and 1980s, advanced amines were introduced for better distribution around the steam cycle and lower corrosion and iron transport; morpholine and ethanolamine are now common in PWRs and PHWRs, and some plants use amine mixtures dictated by condensate polishing needs. EPRI reports [109] that 25 PWRs use ETA, six MPA (methoxypropylamine), four ETA+MPA mixtures, four ETA+DMA (dimethylamine) mixtures, two MPA+DMA mixtures, one DMA alone and one morpholine alone. Users of such amines must consider thermal breakdown products such as acetic acid and formic acid, which can disturb chemistry control and in some conditions affect two-phase FAC [114].

paragraphs.section: 3.2 Cycle Chemistry Treatments for Nuclear Plants
paragraphs.text: For especially vulnerable SGs, for example those tubed with mill-annealed Alloy 600 and so prone to SCC, plants may inject supplementary additives, and boric acid, zinc, titanium and silica have helped in some cases [107]. Dispersants improve blowdown efficiency by keeping particulate corrosion products suspended, polyacrylic acid being a key example applied in some SGs since the 1990s. The need for fully reducing SG conditions and limits on hydrazine because of toxicity have driven a search for alternative reducing agents [115]; candidates like hydroquinone have been examined, but carbohydrazide and diethylhydroxylamine (DEHA) are most common [107], and DEHA trials at Doel 2 in Belgium showed somewhat lower efficiency than hydrazine [115]. As with any complex molecule added to the secondary system, the effects of its thermal breakdown products on SG integrity must be assessed.

paragraphs.section: 3.2 Cycle Chemistry Treatments for Nuclear Plants
paragraphs.text: Although oxygen and oxidizing species must be kept out of the SG, feedwater chemistry may be controlled finely enough to permit relatively high ECP in chosen areas: for example, Germany's Philippsburg PWR injected oxygen against FAC in its steam drain lines [107], and Japan's Tsuruga-2 PWR injected it at the deaerator outlet [108]. AGR boilers with helical tubing inject both oxygen and hydrazine into the feedwater so that materials up to the upper boiler see a relatively high ECP that suppresses FAC, while the temperature rise through the boiler drives the hydrazine-oxygen reaction so that the upper tubing alloy is under reducing conditions [116].

paragraphs.section: 3.2 Cycle Chemistry Treatments for Nuclear Plants
paragraphs.text: Film-forming substances have been used for secondary-side layup protection in PWRs [109], and on-power FFA dosing makes the LP turbine and condenser hydrophobic, reduces the iron carried into the SG and tends to keep particulate corrosion products mobile, improving blowdown efficiency [117]. Yurmanov [118] reported that ODA (octadecylamine) mitigated FAC and improved steam generator performance at the Kola VVER, and corrosion product particles entering the SG apparently become smaller with FFA use [119]. A recent EPRI review [120] of FFAs in nuclear plants, which also covered non-amine film-forming products such as the commercial Anodamine©, concluded that ODA is a promising additive for PWRs and PHWRs because it is the most studied and best understood in nuclear materials and environments, and it highlighted the dangers of FFA overdosing, which creates gelatinous spheroids throughout the system.

paragraphs.section: 4.1 General Remarks on Plant Historical Experiences
paragraphs.text: No official worldwide FAC statistics exist for fossil, combined-cycle or nuclear plants; several unofficial, incomplete surveys have been made during the past three decades at conferences on fossil cycle chemistry and boiler tube failures and at HRSG user group meetings and forums run by the authors. In the nuclear field, FAC papers have appeared roughly every two years at international nuclear plant chemistry conferences since the second Bournemouth conference in 1980, where a paper described FAC in gas-cooled reactors since the cases documented at the Tokai Murai plant in 1968 [121] and also reported erosion-corrosion in the steam-generating parts of sodium-cooled fast breeder reactors. Since Surry in 1986 the US NRC has compiled FAC reports from US plants [13]. These records, plus more than 200 plant FAC assessments by one of the authors, have identified the key FAC locations in power plants and in ACCs; these have not changed in 20 years, and no new system locations under general feedwater conditions have been found anywhere.

paragraphs.section: 4.1 General Remarks on Plant Historical Experiences
paragraphs.text: FAC was found in 1997 in the primary-side feeders of CANDU reactors, carbon steel pipes carrying heavy water coolant from the core to the steam generators, with thinning rates high enough to threaten reactor life, which raised interest in FAC in Canada. Because reactor outlet temperature is about 310 °C, general steel corrosion at those conditions was well documented and the mechanism thought understood, FAC had been regarded as unlikely [122]; its discovery prompted re-examination of accepted mechanisms (Section 2).

paragraphs.section: 4.2 Major FAC Incidents in Generating Plants
paragraphs.text: Table 1 lists the major FAC incidents, all in single-phase water, and deserves close study because of important commonalities across fossil and nuclear plants that can aid initial screening of existing plants and the design/specification of new ones. All cases of aggravated FAC involve high fluid turbulence. The fossil failures happened under AVT(R) feedwater chemistry (Section 3.1), in feedwater systems with all LP and HP feedwater heaters made of stainless steel (usually 304) and with extremely low oxygen (typically below 1 µg · kg^-1), owing either to excellent control of condensate air in-leakage or to the failure location lying downstream of a deaerator. In each, a reducing agent (usually hydrazine) was dosed at the start of the feedwater system, so the failure site was under severe reducing potential.

paragraphs.section: 4.2 Major FAC Incidents in Generating Plants
paragraphs.text: Significantly, the feedwater pH25°C control range was 8.75 to 9.3, most often operated at 9.1 or below, whereas conditions at the failure sites spanned a wide range: 142 to 232 °C (287 to 450 °F) and 0.93 to 20 MPa (134 to 2 900 psi). The bulk of single-phase FAC failures, at locations like economizer inlet header tubes, HP feedwater heater outlets and boiler feedpump outlets (Table 3), were similarly in plants whose feedwater heaters were entirely stainless and which ran AVT(R) under strongly reducing conditions, just like the major incidents [4,123,124].

paragraphs.section: 4.2 Major FAC Incidents in Generating Plants
paragraphs.text: Nuclear secondary systems are mostly kept reducing, with a reducing agent dosed to protect the steam generator and AVT to limit FAC, conditions similar to the fossil cases above. The Table 1 failures at Trojan, Surry and Mihama therefore occurred at 142 to 190 °C (287 to 374 °F), pH25°C 8.6 to 9.3 and oxygen generally below detection, and all under extreme turbulence: at Trojan a fully open globe valve directed flow against the wall that ruptured [11]; at Surry, a 600 mm (24 inch) header discharged into a 450 mm (18 inch) pump suction line immediately before the elbow that failed [12]; and at Mihama, the 558 mm (22 inch) feedwater line ruptured one to two diameters downstream of an orifice plate [16]. These cases underline the importance of regular pipe inspection.

Tables 3 and 4 list the systems in fossil plants typically susceptible to single-phase and two-phase FAC respectively, some locations being prone to both; individual organizations have published similar lists for many years. Such compilations help set the priorities of comprehensive inspection programmes, discussed later.

In combined-cycle plants FAC has been the main cause of HRSG tube failures (HTF) for the past 20 years, accounting for about 35–40 % of all HTFs. Single- and two-phase FAC can both arise in LP and IP evaporators and in LP, IP and HP economizer tubing, though no reliable statistics distinguish the circuits. Two-phase FAC has also affected the steam separation equipment of LP and IP evaporator drums [126] and the riser piping.
