ACCs are fitted to a growing number of fossil and combined-cycle/HRSG plants worldwide. Operating ACC units at the lower pH25°C values allowed in IAPWS guidance [24] leads to serious corrosion and FAC of the ACC tubes, mainly at the cooling tube entries in the upper ducting (streets) [20]. Chemistry-influenced FAC damage in ACCs is best characterized by an index that quantifies the internal FAC condition, the DHACI (Dooley Howell ACC Corrosion Index) [20], recently issued as an ACC Users Group (ACCUG) guideline [127]. The index rates the lower and upper ACC sections separately with a number (1 to 5) and a letter (A to C) after inspection; for example, 3C denotes slight corrosion at the tube entries combined with widespread corrosion in the lower ducts. Figure 26 illustrates the upper section (upper duct/header, A-frame tube entries) and Figure 27 the lower section (turbine exhaust, lower distribution duct, risers).

The DHACI should be recorded at each ACC inspection to describe the unit's FAC history and is very useful for tracking the effect of cycle chemistry changes. For instance, a plant rated poorly (e.g., 4C) at a condensate pH25°C of 8.5–8.8 might raise pH25°C to 9.4–9.6 and check whether its rating improves (e.g., to 3B), while a poor rating (e.g., 4B) signals the need to consider ways of lowering the FAC rate, particularly at tube entries. The DHACI also gives a qualitative indication of total iron corrosion products passing from the ACC into the plant condensate, and serves to compare units with each other and alternative chemistries; several plants worldwide have switched from ammonia to an amine or an FFS and documented the resulting improvements with the DHACI.

Figure 27: montage of DHACI indices A–C for ACC lower ducts from the steam turbine through the vertical risers to the upper duct, higher letters meaning more severe and extensive damage [20].

Nuclear plant issues are usually reported publicly through industry organizations. Responses of US nuclear plants to the USNRC bulletin [13] issued after the Surry rupture showed that all had programmes for inspecting pipe wall thinning in two-phase systems, and most had inspected single-phase systems and started monitoring because of Trojan and Surry. Two-phase FAC appeared in many systems across the plants, and single-phase FAC was widespread in feedwater-condensate systems, especially the recirculation-to-condenser ("minimum-flow") line. Single-phase lines reported: straight runs and fittings of the main feedwater lines and of the main feedwater recirculation line to the condenser; feedwater pump suction lines and discharge lines (straight runs, fittings); condensate booster pump recirculation line fittings; steam generator letdown lines (straight runs, fittings). Reported two-phase lines: main steam lines; turbine cross-over piping; turbine cross-under piping; extraction steam lines; moisture separator reheater; feedwater heater drain piping.

According to [13], six BWRs found wall thinning in feedwater-condensate piping (elbows, reducers, straight runs, recirculation lines), and twenty-six PWRs found it in elbows, reducers, Y-connections, fittings, straight runs, recirculation lines, heater drain piping and drain pump discharge lines, as well as in straight sections after the main feedwater loop isolation valve and after the mini-flow valves of the main feed pumps. Although the USNRC document dates from 1988, the listed systems and components remain vulnerable today (the version on the NRC website was reviewed and updated in 2015, seemingly without changes). In the main feedwater line to the SGs of three Korean PWRs, FAC at the check valve nozzle outlet and the pipe immediately downstream cut wall thickness by up to 40 %, temporarily repaired by weld overlay at one plant and by pipe replacement at the others [128].

A recent WANO (World Association of Nuclear Operators) seminar [129] noted that the Navajo (fossil) and Surry Unit 2 incidents first focused industry attention, followed later by Mihama 3 (Table 1), and listed further fossil failures and these nuclear failures: Arkansas Nuclear One (US) PWR, 1989, two-phase FAC in pipe downstream of a high-pressure extraction nozzle; Santa Maria de Garona (Spain) BWR, 1989, feedwater line blew out after a flow meter under neutral, low-oxygen chemistry; Loviisa Units 1 and 2 (Finland) VVERs, 1990 and 1993, similar through-wall failures in a feedwater orifice flange downstream of the orifice plate, neutral low-oxygen chemistry, flange steel chromium much lower than pipe steel; Millstone 3 (US) PWR, 1990, two parallel lines failed at the same time immediately after control valves fed from the moisture-separator drain tank; Millstone 2 (US) PWR, 1991, failure of reheater drain line piping after a level control valve.

Further nuclear failures cited by the WANO seminar [129]: Sequoyah 2 (US) PWR, 1993, fish mouth rupture of a 275 mm outside diameter pipe downstream of a tee in a high-pressure steam extraction line; Millstone 2 (US) PWR, 1995, FAC downstream of a gate valve in a heater drain line thinned the pipe so that it ruptured in water hammer even though the wall exceeded the minimum; Fort Calhoun (US) PWR, 1997, catastrophic failure of a 5-D sweep in a high-pressure extraction line with the downstream elbow also excessively thinned; Point Beach 1 (US) PWR, 1999, fish mouth failure in the 13 mm wall of a feedwater heater where incoming steam was deflected off the impingement plate onto the shell; Callaway (US) PWR, 1999, 170 mm reheater drain line after a long run where a backing ring disturbed the flow, void fraction 55 %; Susquehanna 1 (US) BWR, 2000, damage to feedwater heater shells, tube supports and tie rods at 142 °C and 91 % steam quality; South Ukraine 2 (Ukraine) VVER, 2005, 45 ° elbow in a 219 mm line from moisture separator tank to deaerator at 211 °C, plus drain line from HP heater to deaerator; Kakrapar 2 (India) PHWR, 2006, 80 mm feedwater line downstream of an orifice. As in fossil plants, chemistry, materials and flow regime effects are clear, and for nuclear plants with limited scope for oxidizing conditions, comprehensive regular monitoring is stressed.

paragraphs.section: 4.7 Surface Appearances of FAC in Generating Plants and Air-Cooled Condensers (ACCs)
paragraphs.text: After the locations of FAC in generating plants and ACCs, this sub-section describes its surface appearance. Determining whether a plant's FAC is single- or two-phase is extremely important for the owner/operator to make the right decisions for reducing the FAC rate, because, as Section 2 explained, different chemistry and hydrodynamic factors govern the two types, and similar conditions in different systems give similar appearances. Hence, for similar materials and chemistries, FAC in nuclear feedwater components looks like that in equivalent fossil components; fossil examples are presented below, together with the distinctive FAC appearance in ACCs, which have no nuclear counterpart.

paragraphs.section: 4.7 Surface Appearances of FAC in Generating Plants and Air-Cooled Condensers (ACCs)
paragraphs.text: Figure 28 presents a pair of single-phase FAC cases from fossil and combined-cycle/HRSG units. Where single-phase FAC is beginning, as near the bottom of photograph A, separate horseshoes or chevrons are clearly visible and always point in the flow direction (bottom to top). As turbulence rises downstream of the bend and the FAC rate grows, toward the middle/top of photograph A, the chevrons overlap to give the typical orange peel appearance of single-phase FAC; chevrons are also evident in photograph B.

paragraphs.section: 4.7 Surface Appearances of FAC in Generating Plants and Air-Cooled Condensers (ACCs)
paragraphs.text: Two-phase FAC in fossil plants is illustrated by the three cases of Figure 29. In the lower photograph the general black/shiny surface, normally easy to spot during inspection, is seen, while the closer views in the upper two photographs reveal dimples within the same black/shiny surface. This contrasts with the directional chevrons and orange peel texture that mark single-phase attack in Figure 28.

paragraphs.section: 4.7 Surface Appearances of FAC in Generating Plants and Air-Cooled Condensers (ACCs)
paragraphs.text: The three HRSG LP evaporator cases in Figure 30 show how distinctive two-phase FAC looks. Among combined-cycle/HRSG plants it is likely the type of FAC most often misdiagnosed, which matters greatly because raising the fluid's oxidizing power will not affect it (Section 2). Established two-phase FAC is always black and shiny (left photograph), and where it is initiating or at the edge of the damage there are often dimples frequently mistaken for pitting corrosion (top right); these usually lack the directionality of single-phase chevrons. As turbulence develops and the wear rate rises, the dimples overlap and the surface may then look like single-phase FAC (Figure 28) but remain black and shiny.

paragraphs.section: 4.7 Surface Appearances of FAC in Generating Plants and Air-Cooled Condensers (ACCs)
paragraphs.text: Figure 31 gives a pair of two-phase FAC cases from fossil deaerators, each located close to where cascading drains from HP feedwater heaters enter and flash against the deaerator surface. The surface is mostly black and shiny, often dimpled as in other two-phase cases such as HRSGs (Figures 29 and 30), visible in the middle of the black shiny area of Figure 31B and just below the drain entry in photograph A. On plants under oxidizing conditions there is usually a very sharp boundary between single-phase flow areas, coloured red under oxidizing conditions, and areas of active two-phase FAC, as in Figures 31B and 32 (left).

paragraphs.section: 4.7 Surface Appearances of FAC in Generating Plants and Air-Cooled Condensers (ACCs)
paragraphs.text: Shells of fossil HP and LP feedwater heaters near the entry of cascading drains from the higher pressure heater are another key two-phase FAC location. In Figure 32, the left photograph (unit on OT, oxidizing) shows black shiny two-phase FAC on a heater shell, with red haematite areas marking single-phase flow regions protected from FAC and black shiny areas where the water/steam mixture from the flashing cascaded drain hits the surface; the right photograph (unit on reducing AVT(R)) shows the two-phase damage as grey/black, darker than the light grey zones where protective magnetite remains.

paragraphs.section: 4.7 Surface Appearances of FAC in Generating Plants and Air-Cooled Condensers (ACCs)
paragraphs.text: These black areas receive no protection because the liquid in the two-phase mixture has no oxidizing power, even though the unit runs on OT with about 150 µg · kg^-1 of oxygen; grey magnetite is also visible under the red haematite. The boundary between protected (single-phase) and unprotected (two-phase) zones is very sharp here, emphasized by the red/black contrast, but it is also seen in units on reducing treatments, where two-phase FAC can be just as severe. The right photograph (AVT(R) unit) shows the darker grey/black two-phase FAC areas, with the worst damage where flash rusting occurred during shutdown, and lighter grey areas where protective magnetite survives.

paragraphs.section: 4.7 Surface Appearances of FAC in Generating Plants and Air-Cooled Condensers (ACCs)
paragraphs.text: Figures 28–32 demonstrate the similarity of single- and two-phase FAC examples between fossil and combined-cycle/HRSG plants. Viewed at higher magnification in an SEM, all plant FAC surfaces, single- or two-phase, are scalloped (four examples in Figure 33), and Figure 20 showed a single-phase nuclear example. Although the scalloping mechanism is not fully understood, the authors always check for this scalloped appearance to confirm FAC as the damage mechanism rather than erosion or cavitation, which do not produce scallops; this check also serves to confirm that laboratory FAC simulations give realistic, plant-like conditions and results.

paragraphs.section: 4.7 Surface Appearances of FAC in Generating Plants and Air-Cooled Condensers (ACCs)
paragraphs.text: Figure 26 gives general views of FAC damage at ACC tube entries, and Figure 34 shows two closer examples from two ACCs, where damage appears as white areas at the tube entries and on the support structure; the white areas on support structures are now thought possibly to result from liquid droplet impingement by larger moisture droplets. Detailed examination of FAC surfaces in ACCs has so far been made on just two tubes taken from two units to characterize FAC surfaces in ACCs [20]; Figure 35 shows details of one. paragraphs.section: 5 Overall Management Approach for FAC in Generating Plants
paragraphs.text: Section 2 detailed FAC mechanisms and Section 4 gave plant examples; cycle chemistry and flow hydrodynamics interact to control FAC and to determine where it occurs, respectively. Mitigating or eliminating FAC damage in steam generating plants needs an overall comprehensive management approach. Such programmes, along with one road map each for conventional fossil and for combined-cycle/HRSG plants, were set out fully in a previous review [18]; they remain valid and are not repeated, but the two road maps are reproduced as Figure 38 as examples and as reference for later sections. For nuclear plants, the OECD Nuclear Energy Agency (NEA) has recently reviewed FAC management programmes in member countries [130] within its CODAP programme (Component Operational Experience, Degradation and Ageing Programme).

paragraphs.section: 5 Overall Management Approach for FAC in Generating Plants
paragraphs.text: These documents, and especially the road maps, make plain that optimizing and monitoring cycle chemistry must never be separated from NDE/inspection in a comprehensive FAC programme. Merely finding FAC locations and treating them superficially (disposition and reassessment, repair, welding, weld overlay) leaves the root cause untouched, which in most cases, particularly in fossil and combined-cycle/HRSG plants, is the cycle chemistry; only optimized cycle chemistry minimizes wall loss and the number of possible FAC sites.

paragraphs.section: 5 Overall Management Approach for FAC in Generating Plants
paragraphs.text: Figure 38: example road maps for the overall approach to mitigate and eliminate FAC, for conventional fossil plants on the left and for combined-cycle/HRSG plants on the right (adapted from [18]); abbreviations PMI = positive metal indication, UT = ultrasonic thickness.

Section 5 established that plant safety depends on an overall, comprehensive FAC programme. As Figure 38 indicates, such a programme must contain both inspection processes and continuous on-line monitoring of total iron, and these two elements are briefly introduced in the sub-sections that follow, first the inspection techniques and then total iron as an FAC indicator.

paragraphs.section: 6.1 Inspection Processes for FAC in Generating Plants
paragraphs.text: Following the overall mitigation approach of Section 5 and Figure 38, after a deterministic analysis (Step 2), or model prediction, has identified possible FAC locations in fossil and combined-cycle plants (typical locations in Tables 3–5), two inspection levels are recommended. Level 1 (Step 7) verifies that FAC is present at a location using methods like fibre optics, pulsed eddy current (PEC) and digital radiography, and Level 2 (Step 8) gives detailed thickness and wear data from gridded ultrasonic thickness (UT) measurements; Table 6 summarizes the techniques with their strengths and weaknesses. Frequent, systematic monitoring of piping and components is essential in nuclear plants, using the same techniques (Table 6). For the primary coolant outlet feeders of PHWRs, intricate intertwined piping in high radiation fields, remote multi-head ultrasonic devices are used that travel around the tight-radius bends near the reactor face.

Ultrasonic Testing: Main Strength=accurate wall thickness reading needed for predicting FAC rate; Main Weakness=low coverage per measurement, needs insulation removal and gridding of pipe or pressure vessel; Proposed Primary Use=Level 2, measurement of wall thickness, successive measurements at long intervals can provide FAC rate. (Digital) Radiographic: Main Strength=volumetric detection, understandable image; Main Weakness=radiation hazard; Proposed Primary Use=Level 1, screening of complex components like valves, pumps, reducers and small bore piping. Visual and Borescopic (Fibre Optics): Main Strength=easily identifies single- and two-phase FAC surface appearances (see sub-section 4.7); Main Weakness=access can be difficult; Proposed Primary Use=Level 1, screening for level control valves, feedwater heater shells and HRSG tubing.

paragraphs.text: As Sections 2 and 4 make clear, for understanding and controlling FAC in fossil and combined-cycle/HRSG plants, one of the most important quantities is the total iron level measured for each plant type and chemistry, which shows whether FAC is under control. Steps 10 and 11 of the FAC programmes in Figure 38 stress how critical it is to know that measured total iron is at a level showing both single- and two-phase FAC to be controlled; Table 7, adapted from IAPWS [23], gives these guidance values.

paragraphs.section: 6.2 Monitoring of Total Iron as an Indicator of FAC
paragraphs.text: To keep shutdown radiation fields low, BWRs add depleted zinc oxide (ZnO with reduced Zn64) to reactor feedwater, the zinc forming a spinel oxide with iron that lowers radioactive cobalt contamination on out-core surfaces. With efficient filtration and condensate polishing, feedwater iron normally stays under 0.5 µg · kg^-1 (ppb) [132] and in several plants under 0.1 µg · kg^-1 (ppb) [108], so core fuel performance is not impaired.

paragraphs.section: 6.2 Monitoring of Total Iron as an Indicator of FAC
paragraphs.text: Feedwater iron in PWRs is usually around 1 µg · kg^-1 (ppb) or lower, with PHWRs at comparable levels. pH control has been proven in Japanese units without copper-bearing alloys, where high pH regimes with ammonia up to pH25°C 10.0 lowered iron to 1 µg · kg^-1 (ppb) from several µg · kg^-1 (ppb), with condensate polishers possibly needing bypass at such high pH [133]. VVERs and French PWRs have also adopted high pH, since pH25°C of 9.2 or less with ammonia alone caused excessive FAC in some units, and 9.5 to 10.0 is commonly reached depending on the amine's volatility and dissociation; condensate polishers have been bypassed or even removed in all-ferrous systems with elevated ammonia [134], and German PWRs have followed a similar approach [135]. Notably, an early sign of excessive FAC in CANDU outlet feeders was a rise in primary coolant temperature to the reactor, mainly from loss of heat transfer efficiency as deposited iron corrosion products fouled the steam generator tube side.

paragraphs.section: 7 The Role of Cycle Chemistry Control and Management in the Mitigation of FAC
paragraphs.text: Recent conferences, publications and assessments show continuing uncertainty about FAC indicators, how single- and two-phase FAC differ, whether FAC is ongoing and whether it can be slowed or stopped by a chemistry change, and what the various surface morphologies and colours mean. Section 2 sought to clarify the mechanisms by describing the theory of oxide growth and of dissolution accelerated by flow hydrodynamics. This section combines the large plant assessment experience (partly shown in Section 4) and detailed knowledge of the IAPWS Cycle Chemistry Guidance [23-26,45,110] with current FAC theory to outline cycle chemistry optimization for FAC mitigation, covering the key features and controlling aspects of FAC mechanisms. Since nuclear FAC control recommendations come from industry/utility organizations worldwide, this section is written as a source document for fossil and combined-cycle plants, though the basic principles apply universally.

paragraphs.section: 7.1 Key Cycle Chemistry Aspects of FAC Mitigation for Conventional Fossil Plants
paragraphs.text: Drawing on current mechanistic understanding (Section 2), plant experience (Section 4) and the authors' reviews of hundreds of organizations' fossil plant FAC programmes worldwide, the key aspects of FAC control in fossil plants (Figure 38) are as follows. Single-phase FAC can be controlled through the potential (ORP) of the feedwater chemistry: it arises under reducing conditions (feedwater oxygen typically below 5 µg · kg^-1 (ppb) plus a reducing agent) where system geometry raises turbulence. In all-ferrous feedwater systems (copper alloys possibly in the condenser), oxidizing treatment (AVT(O) or OT) minimizes corrosion, FAC and hence total iron transport to the boiler; pH25°C should optimally lie between 9.4 and 9.8 [24], the actual value chosen by monitoring total iron against Table 7, and with optimized chemistry levels below 1 µg · kg^-1 (ppb) on OT and below 2 µg · kg^-1 (ppb) on AVT are usually easily achieved.

paragraphs.section: 7.1 Key Cycle Chemistry Aspects of FAC Mitigation for Conventional Fossil Plants
paragraphs.text: In mixed-metallurgy feedwater systems (copper alloys in feedwater heaters and possibly the condenser), reducing treatment (AVT(R)) protects the copper alloys [136], but the connected carbon steel components and pipework also operate reducing and may suffer FAC depending on hydrodynamics (Section 2). Operating at pH25°C 9.1 to 9.3 gives optimum copper alloy protection and limits magnetite dissolution and FAC of carbon steel better than pH25°C below 9.0; the actual optimum should come from monitoring total iron and copper against Table 7, and monitoring has sometimes shown the optimum pH25°C to be above 9.3. On AVT, keeping both total iron and total copper under 2 µg · kg^-1 (ppb) is generally easy with optimized chemistry. The feedwater chemistry must be changed (challenging the status quo) when feedwater heater tube material changes, most commonly from copper alloy to stainless steel tubing; once this covers all LP and HP heaters, FAC risk rises sharply and an immediate switch to oxidizing chemistry with higher pH25°C than in the mixed-metallurgy case is mandatory.

paragraphs.section: 7.1 Key Cycle Chemistry Aspects of FAC Mitigation for Conventional Fossil Plants
paragraphs.text: Monitoring total iron (and copper) indicates, for every feedwater system type, whether chemistry is optimized and FAC controlled, with the IAPWS levels for minimum FAC [23] given in Table 7. Two-phase FAC regions of the feedwater system (deaerators, LP heater shells, Section 4) generally need a materials solution with a 1.25 % Cr or higher alloy (Section 2), whether rebuilding thickness with weld material or replacing equipment; carbon steel weld overlay adds surface roughness and resists FAC no better than the original pressure vessel material. Replacing a component or part in kind is always better than trying to engineer a "better" flow geometry, which experience shows can suffer higher FAC rates than the original.

paragraphs.section: 7.1 Key Cycle Chemistry Aspects of FAC Mitigation for Conventional Fossil Plants
paragraphs.text: The commonest site of two-phase FAC is the cascading drain lines of feedwater heaters after the control valves (Section 4); any thinned or failed part there must be renewed in an alloy of 1.25 % Cr or more. Iron measured in the cascading HP and LP drains frequently reveals how widespread and how active FAC is (Table 7), and total iron below 10 µg · kg^-1 (ppb) is usually easily reached with optimized chemistry. Control valves and downstream piping should always be replaced in chromium-containing material (P11, P22 or P5), and new plants should have these materials designed in at such locations. Two-phase FAC also predominates on HP and LP feedwater heater shells near entries of higher pressure heater drains (Section 4). In addition, all the activities of a comprehensive FAC programme, including prediction, inspection and combined Level 1 and 2 NDE techniques, are needed (Section 5 and Figure 38).

paragraphs.section: 7.2 Key Cycle Chemistry Aspects of FAC Mitigation for Combined-Cycle/HRSG Plants
paragraphs.text: Based on the same sources applied to hundreds of HRSG plant FAC programmes worldwide, the key aspects of FAC control in combined-cycle/HRSG plants (Figure 38) rest on three basic principles: (a) single-phase FAC is prevented only by an oxidizing treatment, AVT(O) or OT [24], and reducing agents are never to be used, whether in operation or shutdown; (b) elevated pH with a volatile amine (up to pH25°C 9.8) is needed to control two-phase FAC [24,25]; and (c) total iron corrosion products should be monitored [23] and compared with Table 7 to verify optimum chemistry. Feedwater and evaporator chemistry can control the single-phase FAC sites (Section 4) [24,25]; multi-pressure HRSGs are to be operated solely on an oxidizing cycle (AVT(O)) without reducing agents, a decision best made at HRSG specification/design, or otherwise as early in HRSG life as possible.

paragraphs.section: 7.2 Key Cycle Chemistry Aspects of FAC Mitigation for Combined-Cycle/HRSG Plants
paragraphs.text: Evaporator chemistry offers a remedy for two-phase FAC in IP and LP evaporator tubes and elsewhere (Section 4): run at high pH25°C with ammonia or an amine [24,45], or add tri-sodium phosphate or NaOH to the LP drum [25] as long as the LP drum does not feed higher pressure HRSG circuits or superheater/reheater attemperation. Some two-phase FAC requires a materials solution (Section 2): where obviously susceptible tube locations exist and chemistry optimization cannot mitigate FAC, they should be renewed in an alloy of 1.25 % Cr or more, and preferably specified in chromium-bearing material at design; the same minimum of 1.25 % Cr steel applies to new or replacement steam separation equipment in the LP/IP drums and to the LP/IP risers.

paragraphs.section: 7.2 Key Cycle Chemistry Aspects of FAC Mitigation for Combined-Cycle/HRSG Plants
paragraphs.text: Iron monitoring in the feedwater and LP drum shows whether FAC is active or consistent with Table 7; meeting the "rule of 2 and 5", with total iron consistently below 2 µg · kg^-1 (ppb) in feedwater and below 5 µg · kg^-1 (ppb) in each drum, indicates FAC is not active [23]. In multi-pressure HRSGs, the HP evaporator deposit level indirectly confirms that total iron in the lower pressure circuits is within the rule of 2 and 5, and removing HP evaporator tubes for deposit analysis also indicates the risk of under-deposit corrosion and hence whether the HRSG needs chemical cleaning [137]. All the activities of a comprehensive FAC programme, including prediction, inspection and combined Level 1 and 2 NDE techniques, are also required (Section 5 and Figure 38).

paragraphs.section: 7.3 Key Cycle Chemistry Aspects of FAC Mitigation for Plants with ACC
paragraphs.text: In fossil and combined-cycle plants, ACCs dictate the required cycle chemistry, and non-optimum chemistry can carry very high corrosion product levels into condensate and feedwater; with low condensate pH (below pH25°C 9.4) iron in the hundreds of ppb has not been unusual, as Figure 39 shows for the ACC of Figure 36. ACCs are a special case within fossil and combined-cycle/HRSG FAC: iron monitoring at the condensate pump discharge is the key indicator of FAC extent and activity at the upper duct tube entries. Worldwide experience shows that cycle pH25°C should at first be set above the range of 9.2 to 9.6 that used to suffice for all-ferrous systems, a condensate pH25°C near 9.8 usually being required, with total iron in line with Table 7.

paragraphs.section: 7.3 Key Cycle Chemistry Aspects of FAC Mitigation for Plants with ACC
paragraphs.text: Figure 39 gives an example, repeated many times worldwide, of the benefit of raising pH for ACC FAC mitigation: during initial OT operation at condensate pH25°C about 9.0, total iron in the condensate was very high (80–100 µg · kg^-1 (ppb)), and as pH25°C was gradually raised over about two years, total iron fell to below 10 µg · kg^-1 (ppb); a condensate filter (5 microns absolute) then keeps iron consistently below 5 µg · kg^-1 (ppb). As Figure 37 shows, growing experience also indicates that dosing an FFS into the ACC ducting gives protection similar to high pH, together with low total iron of 10 µg · kg^-1 (ppb).

paragraphs.section: 7.4 Appearance of Generating Plant Surfaces in Relation to FAC and Flow Regimes
paragraphs.text: The authors have observed uncertainty about the surface features and colours associated with FAC and with FAC that has been mitigated. The Section 4 figures help identify single- and two-phase FAC and show that FAC is local, its sites being set by local flow phenomena and/or geometry that raise turbulence, which the authors call "accentuated turbulent flow" (as found after bends, restrictions and the like); where the flow has recovered to "fully developed turbulent flow", FAC usually falls away to zero. Surface appearances upstream and downstream of the damage, and of the FAC itself, give key visual clues to whether FAC is single- or two-phase and, above all, whether it is active, and this can trigger a focused cycle chemistry review. Table 8 gives an overview of flow regimes and possible chemistries arranged by pH and by oxidizing power or potential (ORP or ECP); its "intensity of fluid dynamics" axis runs from a region where FAC is inactive (first column), to accentuated turbulent flow where FAC occurs (second column), to flow restored to fully developed turbulence (third column).

Accentuated Turbulent Flow=turbulent eddies from geometry (bend, restriction, etc.) locally thin the boundary layer, possible flow separation and reattachment; C. paragraphs.section: 7.5 Assessment of Cycle Chemistry in Controlling FAC in Fossil and Combined-Cycle Plants – Use of Repeat Cycle Chemistry Situation (RCCS) Analysis
paragraphs.text: Understanding of chemistry-influenced FAC mechanisms in conventional fossil and combined-cycle/HRSGs is very advanced and has been documented for over 30 years, with the latest theory given in Section 2. Nevertheless, chemistry-influenced damage and the availability losses from deficient chemistry practice are often huge and can be fatal, and FAC damage and failures persist in fossil, combined-cycle and nuclear units (Section 4), showing that the preventive approaches of operating organizations often fail.

paragraphs.section: 7.5 Assessment of Cycle Chemistry in Controlling FAC in Fossil and Combined-Cycle Plants – Use of Repeat Cycle Chemistry Situation (RCCS) Analysis
paragraphs.text: A concept introduced in 2008 to identify the causes of chemistry-influenced failure and damage, including FAC, and to prevent them proactively [138] is the identification of repeat cycle chemistry situations (RCCS), the basics of cycle chemistry that chemistry or operating staff allow to persist or that are imposed on a plant/organization by inadequate management support for cycle chemistry. Assessment shows that every FAC damage or failure incident traces back to multiple RCCSs that went unrecognized or unaddressed and were allowed to repeat or continue: sometimes chemistry staff missed their importance, and sometimes they saw it but could not convince plant or executive management to act. Plants/organizations can tolerate one or two RCCSs, but as the number grows failure/damage becomes certain.

paragraphs.section: 7.5 Assessment of Cycle Chemistry in Controlling FAC in Fossil and Combined-Cycle Plants – Use of Repeat Cycle Chemistry Situation (RCCS) Analysis
paragraphs.text: There are ten RCCSs in total [138], not all linked to FAC in fossil and combined-cycle plants. Continued RCCS analysis in FAC assessments at nearly 200 plants worldwide shows multiple sub-categories, and where a plant shows over three RCCSs, failure/damage is to be expected and FAC may well be active. To help readers see how RCCSs affect FAC and whether they exist in their own plants, notes on some of the most important FAC-related RCCS categories follow.

paragraphs.section: 7.5 Assessment of Cycle Chemistry in Controlling FAC in Fossil and Combined-Cycle Plants – Use of Repeat Cycle Chemistry Situation (RCCS) Analysis
paragraphs.text: Corrosion Products: total iron monitoring is the key FAC indicator, and Table 7 gives achievable levels for fossil and combined-cycle plants and units with ACC. Indicators of this RCCS include corrosion product levels that are unknown or unmonitored; levels well above international guideline values (Table 7); too few or inadequate monitoring locations; sampling always at the same time/shift; techniques with incorrect detection limits; and, very commonly, monitoring only the soluble part of total iron because samples are not digested. For units on AVT(O), black deposits in the troughs of the steam and water sampling panel (wet rack) are a simple visible confirmation of this RCCS. All these categories are covered in detail in the IAPWS Technical Guidance Document [23].

paragraphs.section: 7.5 Assessment of Cycle Chemistry in Controlling FAC in Fossil and Combined-Cycle Plants – Use of Repeat Cycle Chemistry Situation (RCCS) Analysis
paragraphs.text: Conventional Boiler Waterwall/HRSG Evaporator Deposits: Corrosion products generated by FAC settle on boiler waterwalls or on HRSG HP evaporator tubes, and so indirectly reveal FAC occurring in the cooler, lower pressure sections of the cycle. Indicators include HRSG HP evaporator samples never taken for analysis; no knowledge of HP evaporator deposit levels or deposition rate; samples taken but not comprehensively analysed; deposits exceeding chemical cleaning criteria [137]; HP evaporator deposits not related to lower pressure circuit chemistry or transported total iron [23]; and a sampled HP evaporator needing cleaning while management postpones or cancels it. The IAPWS Technical Guidance Document [137] treats all of these categories in depth for combined-cycle/HRSGs.

paragraphs.section: 7.5 Assessment of Cycle Chemistry in Controlling FAC in Fossil and Combined-Cycle Plants – Use of Repeat Cycle Chemistry Situation (RCCS) Analysis
paragraphs.text: Continuous On-line Cycle Chemistry Instrumentation [26]: Section 2 showed the importance of pH and potential for FAC control and Sections 7.1–7.3 gave the key values for mitigation. Indicators of FAC in a plant include installed and operating instrumentation at a low percentage of IAPWS recommendations [26] (a normal assessed level being 58 to 65 %); many instruments out of service, unmaintained or uncalibrated; instruments not alarmed for operators, with many shared between locations and not/never switched; and plant control relying on grab samples (1 to 3 times per day/shift).

paragraphs.section: 7.5 Assessment of Cycle Chemistry in Controlling FAC in Fossil and Combined-Cycle Plants – Use of Repeat Cycle Chemistry Situation (RCCS) Analysis
paragraphs.text: Challenging the Status Quo: this RCCS is the most important for addressing or preventing FAC in plant cycles. Indicators include no chemistry change since commissioning; incorrect or outdated guidelines; continued use of reducing agents in combined-cycle/HRSGs, risking or experiencing single-phase FAC; continued use of the wrong pH; no chemistry manual for the unit, plant or organization; a wrong chemical addition point (most often reducing agent with AVT(R)); unquestioned use of proprietary chemicals (phosphate blends, amines, FFPs), so that the composition of what is added is unknown; and failure to determine by monitoring the optimum feedwater pH for preventing/controlling FAC.

paragraphs.section: 7.5 Assessment of Cycle Chemistry in Controlling FAC in Fossil and Combined-Cycle Plants – Use of Repeat Cycle Chemistry Situation (RCCS) Analysis
paragraphs.text: RCCS analysis has been used in 197 plant assessments, 118 at conventional fossil plants and 79 at combined-cycle/HRSG plants with HRSGs from 17 manufacturers. Table 9 gives the latest ranking of RCCSs for these plants and shows the same RCCSs appearing in both plant types in roughly the same order, with the four RCCSs most closely tied to FAC, described above, being the most frequent indicators of cycle chemistry problems. This explains why FAC persists despite thorough understanding of the mechanism (Section 2) and well-documented locations (Section 4).

paragraphs.section: 7.5 Assessment of Cycle Chemistry in Controlling FAC in Fossil and Combined-Cycle Plants – Use of Repeat Cycle Chemistry Situation (RCCS) Analysis

FAC continues at a high rate in fossil, combined-cycle and nuclear plants worldwide and remains the leading cause of failure/damage in HRSGs. Although more than 50 years of research have identified all major scientific influences, their application in generating plants has been unsatisfactory: there have been fatalities, and major failures still occur at essentially the same locations as in the 1980s and 1990s (Section 4). Section 2 set out the latest mechanistic theory, and later sections covered main FAC locations, identifying surface features of FAC types, plant cycle chemistries and key monitoring tools. Management should combine inspection, prediction and chemistry into a company-wide coordinated FAC programme within an overall programmatic approach. Cycle chemistry has the dominant influence on both single- and two-phase FAC; the IAPWS Technical Guidance Documents address all major aspects of optimizing it and have been tailored to plant practice (Section 7), and the Section 7 principles apply broadly to nuclear plants, which follow their own industry/utility guidelines.
